Applied and Environmental Microbiology.title: Development and behavior of Steinernema hermaphroditum nematodes are impacted by a bacterial flavin monooxygenase.
Applied and Environmental Microbiology.abstract: Beneficial animal-microbe symbioses occur across the tree of life, with observable impacts on animal development and behavior. The bacterial enzyme complex HpaBC hydroxylates aromatic compounds, which may effect host neurotransmitter-dependent phenotypes. The bacterium Xenorhabdus griffiniae, a beneficial intestinal symbiont of Steinernema hermaphroditum entomopathogenic nematodes, encodes HpaBC. Computational docking of X. griffiniae HpaB substrates showed energetically favorable docking for 4-hydroxyphenylacetate and tyrosine and some affinity for dopamine. We hypothesized that Xenorhabdus HpaBC may influence nematode host development or behavior through its potential action on tyrosine degradation or dopamine catabolism. In support of this idea, we demonstrate a negative correlation between X. griffiniae hpaBC expression and body length and egg-laying behavior in adult S. hermaphroditum nematodes. Moreover, hpaBC expression is necessary for X. griffiniae bacteria to colonize the nematode intestine in the infective juvenile stage. Taken together, these findings indicate that HpaBC may be a part of the metabolic crosstalk occurring between X. griffiniae and S. hermaphroditum at multiple stages of their shared life cycle. hpaBC orthologs are widely present across bacterial phyla, including in pathogens and mutualists of plants and animals. Our findings raise the possibility that HpaBC could be a conserved mechanism by which host-associated bacteria influence physiology and behavior.IMPORTANCEBeneficial animal-microbe interactions can shape development, physiology, and behavior in organisms across the tree of life, yet in many cases, the molecular mechanisms driving these interactions remain poorly understood. This study reveals that the bacterial metabolic enzyme complex HpaBC plays a role in the Steinernema-Xenorhabdus symbiosis, influencing nematode growth, reproduction, and host colonization. As hpaBC expression is conserved across many bacterial phyla, these findings highlight a potentially widespread mechanism for modulating animal physiology through microbial metabolism.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: qPTM 3.0: the AI-enhanced knowledgebase for protein post-translational modification dynamics.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are key mechanisms of regulating protein function, yet quantitative PTM data remain fragmented across publications, supplementary datasets, and specialized resources. Here, we present qPTM 3.0, an integrated resource for quantitative PTM dynamics and AI-assisted knowledge discovery. The current release contains 15 652 063 quantitative events on 994 878 modification sites within 49 280 proteins across 3988 conditions, curated from 846 publications and spanning 12 PTM types in human, mouse, rat, and yeast. Raw mass spectrometry (MS) data associated with the curated entries were re using MaxQuant, and each modification site was assigned a five-star reliability score. Detailed annotations of experimental context, protein information, functional regulation, regulators, and inhibitors are also provided. qPTM 3.0 further introduces two AI-assisted modules. The PTM research agent enables natural-language exploration of qPTM 3.0 and complementary resources by synthesizing evidence on PTM regulators, regulatory conditions, and functional consequences. The data collection agent supports database curation through automated literature screening, full-text retrieval, metadata extraction, quantitative table parsing, and raw MS data acquisition within a human-in-the-loop workflow. Together, these features support systematic exploration of quantitative PTM dynamics and evidence-based biological interpretation. The online service is freely available at https://qptm.omicsbio.info/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Database resources of the National Genomics Data Center, China National Center for Bioinformation in 2027.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The National Genomics Data Center (NGDC), as part of the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB), provides a family of database resources and web services to both academic and industrial communities worldwide. Given the rapid growth of multi-omics data and the intrinsic dependence of artificial intelligence on high-quality curated data, CNCB-NGDC continues to enhance data integrity, usability, and accessibility, facilitate knowledge discovery, and support data-driven research. Over the past year, CNCB-NGDC has expanded and updated its core database resources and strengthened data exchange and sharing with international collaborators. Thirteen new resources have been released, covering genome and variation (HLA and NMVR), health and disease (PWAS Atlas, CoVAR-KG, HONOR, IBDkb, and MTB-ImmunogenKG), biodiversity and biosynthesis (iCellOmics, iPangolin, SesbaniaOmics, and Vita Taxonomy), and tools (π-OmicsKit and DeepSeMS). All resources and services are publicly accessible at https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CellStressDB: an AI-powered database of cellular responses to physical stressors.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Physical stressors profoundly influence cellular behavior by triggering coordinated stress-response programs that regulate signaling, gene expression, metabolism, and cell fate. Here, we present CellStressDB (https://cellstressdb.omic.tech), an AI-powered database for exploring cellular responses to physical stressors. The current release contains data from 131 transcriptomic studies, with 2 364 816 cell and 1205 bulk sample observations from human and mouse across nine physical-stress classes and 21 tissue categories. Data and analyses are organized into 2848 indexed analysis entries across 71 canonical species-tissue-stress contexts with detailed exposure conditions retained. CellStressDB provides ontology-guided cell-type annotation through 22 tissue-aware classifiers and incorporates 941 Geneformer checkpoints for context-specific in silico perturbation. Analyses include stress-response programs, differential gene expression, functional enrichment, regulon activity, cell-type composition, and cell-cell communication where applicable, with candidate compound prioritization, downloadable datasets and models, and analysis of user-provided transcriptomic data. Annotation evaluation and known-factor recovery analyses indicated context-dependent performance and coverage across biological settings. The mouse radiation-intestine example identifies Stat1 as a candidate regulator of radiation-induced intestinal injury supported by independent experimental evidence. Overall, CellStressDB provides an integrated, AI-enabled framework for exploring and interpreting cellular responses to physical stressors and generating testable hypotheses.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: X-BCRdb: a cross-disease BCR-paired single-cell database for B-lineage-cell clonotype-transcriptome analysis.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: B cells and their clonally rearranged B-cell receptors (BCRs) form the cellular and molecular basis of humoral immunity. Single-cell RNA sequencing coupled with V(D)J profiling now enables BCR clonotypes to be linked directly to B-cell transcriptional states; however, existing immune-receptor resources are often T-cell/TCR-oriented or limited in BCR-specific analytical depth. Here, we present X-BCRdb, a cross-disease single-cell database for integrated analysis of BCR repertoires, B-cell transcriptional states, and clonal evolution. The current release harmonizes 61 studies, 1401 samples, and 903 subjects across 45 disease or physiological categories and 13 tissue groups. It contains 2 402 995 processed B-lineage cells, including 1 565 870 cells with matched transcriptome and BCR information, and 3 993 244 annotated BCR records. A unified analytical workflow supports standardized B-cell annotation and BCR repertoire characterization, including clonotype assignment, SHM profiling, isotype analysis, VH/VL pairing, lineage reconstruction, and public clonotype analysis. The web interface links these receptor features with B-cell transcriptional states across individual samples, studies and diseases, and provides global CDR3 similarity search, data download, and API access. X-BCRdb is freely available at https://xbcrdb.net/ and provides a systematic platform for studying disease-associated B-lineage-cell responses and facilitating the prioritization of candidate BCR sequences for downstream antibody discovery and functional validation.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: tRNA database 2026, extended compilation of tRNA sequences and tRNA genes.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The tRNAdb database, published >15 years ago, originated as an extension of Mathias Sprinzl's seminal collection of transfer RNA (tRNA) data dating back to the late 1970s. Throughout its lifespan, the tRNAdb has been used extensively, accumulating >1000 citations. Here, we present tRNAdb 2026, https://tdb.bioinf.uni-leipzig.de/, an updated version hosted at Leipzig University. The tRNAdb 2026 features an ~10-fold increase in data coverage, containing >500 000 new mitochondrial and nuclear tRNA sequences together with the unaltered legacy dataset. Importantly, identifiers and metadata of the legacy dataset remain consistent with the original database, ensuring that previously published references remain valid and findable. The expanded dataset integrates publicly available tRNA annotations and sequences generated using contemporary prediction pipelines followed by semiautomated curation to ensure annotation quality and consistency. In addition, cross-references to external resources such as gtRNAdb facilitate interoperability with existing tRNA annotation frameworks. A modern web-based frontend provides intuitive and efficient access to tRNAdb 2026, while an Application Programming Interface enables automated data retrieval and integration into bioinformatics workflows. To support transparent scientific documentation and reproducibility across future updates, we added a versioning system for both current and future database releases.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: miRPathDB 2027: an updated multi-species atlas of microRNA-pathway associations.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Pathway enrichment helps interpret the many genes targeted by microRNAs (miRNAs), but comparisons across organisms are complicated by differences in target evidence and functional annotation. Here, we present miRPathDB 2027, which extends miRPathDB from human and mouse to rat and rhesus macaque. Its retained enrichment profiles span 5701 miRNA entries and 28 044 pathway and ontology accessions from Gene Ontology, Reactome, and WikiPathways. Three cumulative evidence tiers allow users to examine how associations change as broader experimental records and computational predictions are included. Cross-species views align curated miRNA families, separated by mature arm, with corresponding pathway terms and indicate unavailable comparisons; a prespecified analysis tests whether orthologous miRNA profiles agree more than expected from matched random target sets. Interactive miRNA and pathway profiles, heat maps, versioned downloads, and programmatic access connect these patterns to the underlying targets and evidence. miRPathDB 2027 supports exploration of miRNA function and prioritization of associations for experimental follow-up. The database web interface is freely available without registration at https://web.ccb.uni-saarland.de/mirpathdb/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: HIPPIE 3.0: expanding experimental evidence for mining and predicting protein interaction networks.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are central to cellular function, disease gene identification, and therapeutic targeting. Human Integrated Protein-Protein Interaction rEference (HIPPIE) provides a confidence-scored reference network of experimentally supported human PPIs by integrating evidence from multiple resources and assigning reliability scores to individual interactions. Here, we present HIPPIE 3.0, a major update that substantially expands the scale and scope of the resource. HIPPIE now contains ~1.2 million experimentally supported PPIs, a fourfold increase since the last major release, including 71 000 isoform-specific interactions. Beyond interaction data, HIPPIE captures the underlying experimental search space by incorporating non-interacting protein pairs experimentally tested, and provides large-scale cross-species conservation annotations. This release expands the catalog of experimental methods, recalibrates confidence scores, and introduces a redesigned web interface that improves data access and exploration. To support machine learning applications, HIPPIE 3.0 provides high-confidence positive interactions and negative training datasets, together with tools for generating sequence-similarity- and degree-aware benchmark splits to reduce performance inflation caused by data leakage. By combining an expanded experimental interactome with benchmark-generation strategies tailored for PPI prediction, HIPPIE 3.0 serves as both a reference interactome and a platform for evaluating PPI prediction methods. HIPPIE 3.0 is freely available at hippie-db.net.

mSystems.title: Genomic characterization of greenhouse-associated Aspergillus fumigatus from China reveals population structure, antifungal resistance, and relationships with global lineages.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Aspergillus fumigatus is a globally distributed saprophyte and a major opportunistic pathogen causing invasive aspergillosis. The emergence of azole-resistant A. fumigatus in agricultural environments poses a growing threat to human health, yet the genetic basis of resistance and the role of agricultural hotspots remain poorly understood. Here, we analyzed 226 greenhouse-derived isolates from Yunnan, China, within a global genomic framework. Although Yunnan isolates shared overall diversity patterns with worldwide populations, they exhibited pronounced population structure, with one well-supported clade (Clade B) enriched in greenhouse environments. To investigate cross-environment relationships, we further analyzed an expanded collection of isolates from greenhouse soils, air, agricultural markets, and clinical sources using multilocus genotyping. Identical or highly similar genotypes were detected across environments, including resistant strains carrying the TR₃₄/L98H allele, demonstrating that greenhouse and clinical isolates are genetically connected. Genome-wide association analyses identified candidate loci associated with antifungal resistance and stress tolerance beyond canonical cyp51A mutations, including genes involved in cell wall remodeling and mitochondrial dynamics. Together, these results reveal the genomic landscape of greenhouse-associated A. fumigatus in China and provide evidence for genetic connectivity between agricultural and clinical settings, underscoring the importance of surveillance at agricultural-clinical interfaces. [IMPORTANCE] Azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus is an increasing global health concern because resistant infections are difficult to treat and often fatal. Agricultural environments have been implicated as important sources of resistance, yet the mechanisms underlying the emergence, persistence, and transfer of resistance to human patients remain unclear. By integrating genomic and phenotypic analyses of greenhouse-derived isolates from Yunnan, China, we identified a distinct clade that is enriched in greenhouse environments and exhibits stable antifungal resistance. Resistant genotypes were repeatedly detected across greenhouses, local markets, and patients; notably, identical multilocus genotypes and cyp51A mutations were shared between market air samples and a patient with invasive aspergillosis, demonstrating genetic connectivity between agricultural and clinical settings. Beyond the well-known cyp51A mutations, genome-wide association analyses highlighted several candidate loci associated with antifungal resistance-including a dynamin-related GTPase and a strongly induced cell-wall peptidase-that may represent non-canonical resistance mechanisms. These findings provide insights into fungal adaptation and resistance evolution in agricultural contexts. They underscore the urgent need for integrated surveillance and stewardship across agricultural and medical sectors to mitigate the spread of antifungal resistance.

mSystems.title: Microbiota-dependent citrulline metabolism alleviates sepsis by activating the aryl hydrocarbon receptor/IL-22 pathway to restore intestinal homeostasis.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] This study investigated whether citrulline ameliorates sepsis-associated immune inflammation and intestinal barrier injury by modulating gut microbiota metabolites. Using an in vitro co-culture system and a cecal ligation and puncture mouse model, we found that citrulline fermentation products significantly increased the production of short-chain fatty acids and indole derivatives. These metabolic changes activated the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathway, upregulated interleukin-22 (IL-22) secretion, STAT3 phosphorylation, and restored the Treg/Th17 cell balance. Consequently, intestinal barrier function was improved, as evidenced by enhanced expression and membrane localization of tight junction proteins, and increased antimicrobial peptide production. Inhibition of AhR or STAT3 weakened the immunoregulatory and barrier-restorative effects of citrulline fermentation products in vitro. In vivo, citrulline treatment improved sepsis severity scores, reduced intestinal neutrophil infiltration, attenuated intestinal mucosal injury, increased goblet cell numbers, and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines while increasing IL-10 levels in serum. Citrulline also alleviated CLP-induced lung and liver inflammatory injury. These protective effects were diminished by antibiotic treatment or AhR inhibition. RNA sequencing analysis confirmed that citrulline activates AhR and IL-22-responsive barrier gene programs while suppressing NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling. In conclusion, citrulline modulates the gut microbial metabolic environment to activate the AhR/IL-22/STAT3 axis, thereby rectifying immune imbalance, restoring intestinal integrity, and alleviating systemic inflammation in sepsis. These findings provide a novel theoretical foundation for nutritional and immune interventions in sepsis management. [IMPORTANCE] Sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection, often damages the gut, leading to a vicious cycle of inflammation and organ failure. While gut bacteria are known to influence health, how specific nutrients shape their protective effects in sepsis is unclear. This study reveals that the amino acid citrulline acts as a fuel for beneficial gut bacteria. When these bacteria metabolize citrulline, they produce molecules that act as signals to the body's immune system. These signals help calm harmful inflammation, repair the gut lining, and restore immune balance during sepsis. Our findings identify citrulline not just as a nutrient, but as a targeted regulator of the gut-immune axis, offering a promising new dietary strategy to support sepsis treatment by working with the body's microbial allies.

mSystems.title: Gut microbiome and metabolomics reveal the role of thioproline in attenuating colorectal cancer-associated inflammation.
mSystems.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the top three cancers globally in terms of both incidence and mortality, and its development may be influenced by an inflammatory environment in the intestines, often associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis. Food bioactives could modulate gut microbiota through anti-inflammatory and epigenetic mechanisms. Given the significant role of thioproline as a food bioactive with antioxidant properties, its potential to modulate gut microbiota and mitigate CRC remains largely unexplored. This study aims to understand the effects of thioproline on gut microbiota community and investigate the mechanisms through which thioproline regulates gut microbiota and exerts its anticancer effects. Fecal and intestinal tissue samples were collected from health, CRC, and thioproline-treated CRC mice. The metagenome and metabolome data revealed that thioproline treatment significantly altered the gut microbiota community composition and metabolism in CRC mice. These CRC-associated gut microbiota and bacterial metabolites returned to normal levels. Moreover, under thioproline treatment, the microbial-metabolite interactions in CRC mice shifted toward patterns more closely resembling those observed in healthy mice. Thioproline treatment increased linoleic acid levels in mice, indicating its role in promoting linoleic acid metabolism to therapeutically restore homeostasis and alleviate inflammation in CRC. This was further supported by hematoxylin and eosin staining, which demonstrated that thioproline alleviated inflammation in CRC mice. Our study highlights thioproline's dual role in regulating the gut microbiota community and bacterial metabolism, modulating bacteria-host interactions, and ultimately reducing inflammation in CRC. These findings offer valuable insights for future research and therapeutic applications.IMPORTANCEColorectal cancer (CRC) is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis and intestinal inflammation. While food bioactives can modulate the microbiome, whether thioproline exerts inhibitory effects against CRC through microbial regulation remains unknown. Using integrated metagenomics and metabolomics, we show that thioproline treatment restores the gut microbiota composition and bacterial metabolites disrupted by CRC to near-normal levels. Importantly, thioproline remodels microbial metabolite interaction networks, elevates linoleic acid levels, and alleviates intestinal inflammation. This study provides a systems-level perspective on how a single dietary bioactive compound reshapes the gut microbial ecosystem and its metabolic landscape to reduce inflammation in CRC. Our findings suggest a potential role for microbiome-targeted nutritional strategies in protecting against CRC progression through modulation of the gut microbiota and intestinal microenvironment.

mSystems.title: Nutrient control enables metabolic reconstruction of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG and analysis of secretions.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) is an important gut commensal bacterial strain that has been extensively studied in both industrial and health settings. Despite its long history of study, a high-quality genome-scale metabolic network model (GEM) for LGG has yet to be reconstructed. Only automatically generated draft models have been published, which have notoriously limited functional accuracy. Furthermore, comprehensive nutrient requirements have not been established for well-controlled in vitro studies. Here, we present the first curated GEM for LGG using a new approach for reconstruction and validation that leverages multiple automatically generated draft models, applied study literature, and high-throughput defined media experiments. In addition, our results include a series of chemically defined media, extensive single-component nutrient dropout growth data, insights from in silico and in vitro experiments into secretion products, lactate, and indole-3-carboxaldehyde, a minimal medium, and in silico characterization of LGG's nutrient requirements. Our approach for developing interdisciplinary research tools for LGG metabolism comprises a new framework that could be applied to many understudied microorganisms, particularly useful in studying bacteria within the human microbiome. [IMPORTANCE] This study provides an important foundation for understanding how the beneficial gut bacterium Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) grows and interacts with its environment. Although LGG is one of the most widely studied probiotic bacteria, used in both health and industrial applications, a reliable tool for simulating its metabolic behavior and a clear understanding of its nutritional needs is lacking. By developing the first manually curated metabolic model of LGG and validating it through extensive laboratory experiments, this study provides new understanding of LGG's requirements and capabilities for utilizing nutrients and resources to investigate its metabolism. Completely chemically defined growth media and associated single-component dropout growth effects are also presented, and pathways for production of important compounds influencing human health are explored. The methods developed in this work also provide a framework for studying other poorly characterized microbes, helping advance research on the human microbiome and its role in health and disease.

mSystems.title: A plasmid-encoded H-NS protein selectively binds its own plasmid.
mSystems.abstract: H-NS is an abundant nucleoid-associated protein found in Enterobacterales species. Some conjugative plasmids encode H-NS homologs, which are thought to facilitate plasmid maintenance and reduce the fitness costs associated with plasmid carriage. Here, we characterize HppXCROD2, an H-NS homolog encoded by the IncX4 plasmid pCROD2 of Citrobacter rodentium. Our data indicate that HppXCROD2 has a strong preference for binding pCROD2 over the chromosome, or other plasmids. By contrast, chromosomally encoded H-NS displays no preference for plasmid sequence. When expressed from a heterologous plasmid in Escherichia coli, HppXCROD2 showed similar DNA-sequence preference to chromosomally encoded H-NS. Moreover, HppXCROD2 binding to a sequence from pCROD2 was much lower when that sequence was cloned in a laboratory plasmid. Thus, HppXCROD2 preferentially binds DNA in the context of the plasmid where it is encoded, a phenomenon we term "cognate plasmid specificity." We propose that cognate plasmid specificity occurs through recognition of plasmid-specific DNA topology generated by plasmid-encoded topoisomerases. Cognate plasmid specificity may insulate regulation of plasmid genes from the effects of host DNA, while minimizing disruption of host chromosome regulation due to plasmid carriage.IMPORTANCEMany bacteria carry conjugative plasmids, mobile DNA molecules that spread traits such as antibiotic resistance. Some conjugative plasmids encode proteins related to the bacterial DNA-binding protein H-NS. We show that an H-NS-like protein from the IncX4 plasmid pCROD2 binds almost exclusively to the plasmid from which it originates, while largely ignoring the host chromosome. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism that allows plasmids to regulate their own genes with high specificity while minimizing interference with host gene expression.

mSystems.title: Evolutionary histories of microbial calcification-associated genes across the tree of life.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Biocalcification, a widespread process by which animals and algae form hard tissues and cellular structures, has played a major role in the global carbon cycle over the past 541 Ma. Extracellular or intracellular carbonates are formed by diverse bacteria, yet the genetic basis and evolutionary history of this process remain poorly resolved. Here, we present a large-scale survey of an intracellular calcification marker (calcyanin) and two calcification-associated genes with potential mineralization-promoting roles (carbonic anhydrase [CA] and urease) across the Bacteria and Archaea domains. High-sequence-coverage homologs of calcyanin are restricted to oxygenic cyanobacteria and consistent with vertical inheritance within seven families, suggesting a possible origin in a common ancestor of the Cyanobacteriia class, although some cases likely reflect horizontal gene transfer (HGT). In contrast, CA genes are widespread across all domains of life, with phylogenetic and structural analyses supporting independent origins of the α-, β-, and γ-classes, followed by extensive inter-phylum and possible inter-domain HGT events. Urease genes are distributed broadly and most likely originated in Pseudomonadota or Cyanobacteriota, and their phylogenetic placement is consistent with extensive bacterial and archaeal diversification and a possible bacterial contribution to plant and fungal ureases. Together, these findings not only reveal distinct evolutionary trajectories of microbial calcification-associated genes but also provide a genomic framework for generating hypotheses that microbial calcification may have interacted with ocean chemistry and the global carbon cycle since the Archaean. [IMPORTANCE] Microbes help regulate the global carbon cycle partly by influencing when and where carbonate minerals form on Earth's surface. However, the genes connected to microbial calcification have not been evaluated broadly across the bacterial and archaeal tree of life or in relation to early Earth history. Here, we analyze a previously experimentally validated intracellular calcification marker and two widespread enzymes that can influence carbonate chemistry under suitable conditions. Our results show that these gene systems have distinct and complex evolutionary histories, including inheritance within lineages, gene loss, duplication, transfer between distantly related microbes, and possible transfers between bacteria and eukaryotes. Compared with previous taxon- or gene-specific studies, this work provides a broader evolutionary view of how mineralization-promoting functions emerged, diversified, and spread across microbial lineages. It provides a genomic framework for studying how microbial physiology may have interacted with ocean chemistry and carbon cycling through Earth history.

mSystems.title: Transposable element content is associated with total genome size and host taxonomy in sulfur-oxidizing bacterial endosymbionts.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile genetic sequences that can disrupt, relocate, or create genes and regulatory elements, thereby contributing to genome evolution. Their potential role in shaping adaptation, including symbiotic relationships, has drawn increasing attention. Most research on TEs to date has focused on terrestrial environments, while less is known about TE function and prevalence in marine habitats. This study investigates the presence and distribution of TEs in marine chemosynthetic symbioses, specifically among the genomes of sulfur-oxidizing Gammaproteobacteria associated with animals living in a diversity of chemically reducing environments. Our data reveal that factors such as phylogenetic relationship and habitat type have no demonstrated association with TE abundance, while factors such as genome size, host family, and lifestyle are significantly correlated. Almost all vesicomyid clam symbionts lacked TEs likely because of reductive genome evolution, while mytilid symbionts had the highest TE abundance possibly due to increased rates of homologous recombination or TE proliferation related to adaptive genome streamlining. Transposase family diversity varied considerably among symbiont groups but was not associated with genome size, indicating that other factors influence transposase composition. Notably, a large fraction of transposase genes was flanked by genes involved in DNA replication and repair, membrane transport, and prokaryotic defense systems, implying a possible role in environmental or host adaptation. This study highlights the dynamic nature of TE content in symbiotic bacteria and allows for the formulation of hypotheses on TE function for the evolution of bacteria in diverse, chemically reducing environments. [IMPORTANCE] Transposable elements are key drivers of bacterial genome evolution and environmental adaptation by creating new gene functions and altering existing ones, yet they remain comparatively understudied in marine microbes. In this study, we assessed TE content and the function of flanking genes in symbiotic and free-living sulfur-oxidizing bacteria from a variety of aquatic environments. Our analyses show that genome size, bacterial lifestyle, and host association have a significant impact on TE abundance, but not necessarily transposase diversity. Transposases were often flanked by DNA replication and repair genes, membrane transporters, and prokaryotic defense systems, which likely represent transposition cargo that might be relevant for habitat adaptation. The patterns observed within these data further our understanding of the distribution and function of transposases and lay a foundation for future studies investigating the role of transposases in bacterial genome evolution.

mSystems.title: Gut microbiota-associated metabolic alterations contribute to 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction in mice.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] N-(1,3-Dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine quinone (6PPD-Q), a ubiquitous tire-derived contaminant detected in environmental matrices and human samples, poses potential intestinal health risks to mammals. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice were orally exposed to 6PPD-Q (4 mg/kg, once every 3 days for 28 days) with or without broad-spectrum antibiotic pretreatment to deplete gut microbiota. 16S rRNA sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, immunofluorescence, and periodic acid-Schiff staining were performed to characterize microbial, metabolic, and intestinal barrier alterations. 6PPD-Q exposure induced gut dysbiosis characterized by enrichment of Lachnospiraceae and depletion of Akkermansiaceae and Bacteroidaceae accompanied by alterations in tryptophan and nicotinate-nicotinamide metabolism, including reduced fecal serotonin and indole-3-propionic acid levels. Furthermore, 6PPD-Q exposure impaired intestinal barrier integrity, as evidenced by altered expression of tight junction proteins (ZO-1 and claudin-1), reduced goblet cell density, and decreased MUC2 expression. Notably, antibiotic-mediated microbiota depletion attenuated 6PPD-Q-associated microbial, metabolic, and intestinal barrier alterations, suggesting that gut microbiota contribute to 6PPD-Q-associated intestinal responses. Collectively, this study provides mechanistic insights into microbiota-associated mechanisms underlying 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier alterations and advances understanding of potential health implications of tire-derived emerging contaminants. [IMPORTANCE] 6PPD-Q, a primary oxidation product of the rubber antioxidant 6PPD, is an emerging environmental pollutant widely detected in human blood and urine. While its systemic toxicity has been recognized, the role of the gut microbiota in mediating 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier disruption remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that gut microbiota plays an important modulatory role in 6PPD-Q-induced intestinal barrier impairment using antibiotic depletion and mouse models. Multi-omics analyses revealed that 6PPD-Q altered the composition of gut commensals and disrupted metabolic homeostasis, while functional validation confirmed its impact on epithelial integrity. Our findings identify the gut microbiota as a key modulator of 6PPD-Q toxicity and provide novel mechanistic insights into the environmental health risks of tire-derived pollutants.

mSystems.title: Phylogeography of clinical Burkholderia pseudomallei isolates in Cambodia demonstrates diversity, broad dispersal, and novel genes.
mSystems.abstract: Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative agent of melioidosis, is ubiquitous in Southeast Asia but remains understudied in many endemic countries. The species' high genetic diversity necessitates large-scale sampling to resolve fine-scale population structure. In countries bordering the Mekong River, the geographic range of B. pseudomallei strains may be increased by water-mediated dispersal. Between 2021 and 2023, we collected and sequenced 253 clinical B. pseudomallei isolates from patients admitted to six Cambodian hospitals and geotagged isolates by patient village. Isolates were genetically diverse and grouped into 11 clades, including one characterized by a chromosomal genomic island containing unique genes absent from other isolates, consistent with local evolution. Comparison with 3,234 publicly available global genomes revealed intermixing between Cambodian and other Southeast Asian isolates but clear distinction from Australian strains. Phylogeographic analyses further demonstrated spatial localization along major waterways, suggesting that river systems, including the Mekong, may contribute to bacterial dissemination in Cambodia. Taken together, these findings demonstrate the importance of localized data sets for contextualizing the population structure and evolution of this diverse pathogen in Southeast Asia.IMPORTANCEBurkholderia pseudomallei is a highly diverse bacterial species with genomic features that vary based on geographic sampling location. Existing data predominantly from Thailand show that isolates from Southeast Asia may be closely related to each other. Here, we sequenced isolates associated with human disease in Cambodia and compared these against genomes from public sequence repositories. We identified many distinct bacterial strains and found that some of these were localized either to the south or in the north of the country. We identified a unique group of genes in one cohort strain with putative roles in bacterial metabolism and genomic recombination. Finally, in a global phylogeny constructed from publicly available genomes, we found that Cambodian isolates intermixed with other Southeast Asian isolates. Our study is the largest genomic study of B. pseudomallei in Cambodia to date, with findings that contribute to the global understanding of the bacterium's diversity and evolution.

mSystems.title: Differential impacts of early, extended-spectrum, and last-resort β-lactams on manure-derived microbiomes and resistomes in an in vitro model.
mSystems.abstract: Understanding the environmental dissemination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is crucial for mitigating its spread and reducing the clinical burden of resistant infections. In a previous study, we demonstrated that copiotrophic enrichment in a medium that stimulates the growth of gut-associated bacteria can reveal clinically associated bacterial populations and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) that are not detected through direct environmental sampling. In the present study, we applied this enrichment approach to poultry manure to examine how β-lactamase-resistant antibiotics (cefotaxime and meropenem) shape the composition and resistance profiles of copiotrophic, gut-like microbial community relative to an earlier β-lactam (ampicillin) and to antibiotic-free controls. Our results show that extended-spectrum and last-resort β-lactams induced more pronounced shifts in microbial diversity, resistome, and mobilome profiles compared to ampicillin. When focusing on specific taxa, such as clinically relevant enteric bacteria and both susceptible and β-lactam-resistant coliforms, differential responses were observed correlating to the antimicrobial range of action. Moreover, cefotaxime and meropenem exerted different effects on the relative abundance of enteric bacteria and plasmids harboring multiple ARGs. Together, these findings underline how the diversity of pathogen and AMR indicators in gut microbiomes may be shaped by different selective pressures imposed by β-lactamase-resistant antibiotics.IMPORTANCEThis study explores how different generations of β-lactam antibiotics shape microbial communities and antibiotic resistance in a gut-like in vitro system. Using a metabolically driven synthetic community derived from manure, we found that advanced β-lactams such as cefotaxime and meropenem led to stronger and more specific shifts in both community composition and resistance gene profiles compared to ampicillin. These results emphasize that the ecological impact of antibiotics depends not only on whether bacteria are inhibited but also on the spectrum of activity of each compound. In addition, the system we used provides a simple and controllable way to study interactions among antibiotics, microbial communities, and the resistome. Overall, this work offers a clearer ecological view of how clinically important antibiotics may influence microbiomes and the spread of antibiotic resistance genes.

mSystems.title: Auxiliary glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenases shape central carbon metabolism in Pseudomonas putida.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenases (GapDHs) are key enzymes in central carbon metabolism, yet their functional diversity extends beyond canonical glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. The soil bacterium Pseudomonas putida KT2440 encodes four GapDH isoenzymes (i.e., GapA, GapB, GapC, and GapD). GapA and GapB have been recently described as gatekeepers of metabolic segregation, with GapA driving glycolysis and GapB associated with gluconeogenesis. However, the physiological roles of GapC and GapD remain poorly defined. In this work, we combined targeted mutagenesis, growth phenotyping, in vitro biochemical analysis, proteomics, and metabolomics to dissect the functions of these lesser-studied GapDH isoforms. GapC and GapD have distinct structural features, diverging from the canonical GapA and GapB enzymes. Physiological characterization of gap-deletion mutants of P. putida across multiple glycolytic and gluconeogenic substrates showed that GapC and GapD exert substrate-specific effects and contribute to network-wide redox balancing. Proteomic and metabolomic profiling further indicated that GapC and GapD are integrated into specialized metabolic modules, supporting auxiliary functions that complement the dominant roles of GapA and GapB. This case of metabolic redundancy at the GapDH node highlights the versatility of central carbon metabolism in bacteria adapted to changing environmental conditions. [IMPORTANCE] Bacteria often carry multiple isoenzymes for the same metabolic step, yet the reasons for such redundancy remain poorly understood. By dissecting the roles of GapDH isoforms in P. putida, we show that these enzymes are not functionally equivalent but rather partition their activity across glycolytic, gluconeogenic, and auxiliary functions. GapC and GapD provide secondary capacity under specific conditions that complement the known roles of GapA and GapB, which dominate glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, respectively. Growth phenotyping, together with proteomic and metabolomic analyses, revealed that isoenzyme specialization is reflected in both substrate-dependent abundance patterns and metabolite profiles. This study underscores the evolutionary diversification of central metabolic enzymes in environmental bacteria and their coordinated regulation across nutritional states. Furthermore, our findings provide a framework for engineering carbon flux in Pseudomonas and related bacteria, with implications for metabolic engineering applications targeting diverse feedstocks.

mSystems.title: MIMEco: multi-objective metabolic modeling to predict and explain pairwise interactions.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Genome-scale metabolic models provide a mechanistic framework for quantitatively exploring an organism's physiology and its interactions with the environment. However, their use in microbial community modeling has been limited since it usually relies on community-wide objective functions or the integration of community abundance data. Nevertheless, predicting microbial interactions is crucial for understanding ecosystem dynamics and thus requires dedicated methods. Here, we introduce Metabolic Interaction Modeling in Ecosystems (MIMEco), an open-source Python package that predicts pairwise microbial interactions through multi-objective optimization. MIMEco does not require abundance data, provides a user-friendly workflow, and predicts interaction types, strengths, and exchanged metabolites directly from Pareto fronts. In this study, MIMEco is validated by replicating experimental results of an in vitro co-culture of two auxotrophic Escherichia coli strains. By combining mechanistic inference with usability, MIMEco makes metabolic interaction modeling accessible to non-specialists while remaining flexible for experts, establishing a versatile platform for advancing metabolic ecology across biomedical and environmental fields. [IMPORTANCE] Deciphering microbial interactions through in vitro experiments is often costly and limited in scope, while existing bioinformatics tools can be complex to use or limited by actual sample data. Metabolic Interaction Modeling in Ecosystem (MIMEco) offers an open-source and user-friendly multi-objective framework for predicting and quantifying pairwise microbial ecosystem interactions and nutrient exchanges. We demonstrate its reliability by replicating a well-characterized laboratory experiment, showing that MIMEco can accurately reflect real biological behavior. This tool improves the community's ability to explore and understand metabolic interaction mechanisms underpinning microbial ecosystems.

mSystems.title: Non-redundant cardiolipin synthase family proteins shape lipid composition and stress resilience in Bacteroides fragilis.
mSystems.abstract: Gut-resident bacteria must withstand membrane-disrupting stresses, such as bile acids, to persist in the intestinal environment. The Bacteroidota are a dominant phylum of the human gut microbiota. However, the genes responsible for the synthesis of membrane lipids in this phylum remain relatively uncharacterized. Bacteroides fragilis is a prevalent member of this phylum and encodes two predicted cardiolipin synthase family proteins, ClsA and ClsB. We previously identified both cls genes as bile-acid fitness factors in B. fragilis P207, but the contributions of clsA and clsB to cell physiology remained unclear. Here, we combine targeted gene deletion with high-resolution lipidomics, metabolomics, and elemental mass spectrometry to show that ClsA and ClsB have distinct and non-redundant functions in the cell. Each cls gene differs in its growth-phase expression pattern, and deletion of each gene produces distinct effects on cell morphology, fitness under membrane-perturbing stress, and the broader metabolome. clsA and clsB strongly influence the levels of different glycyl-seryl peptidolipids, a Bacteroides lipid family that includes immune-active lipids, and whose loss impairs bile acid resistance and gut colonization. In contrast to the acute ion-gradient disruption caused by the secondary bile acid deoxycholate, deletion of clsA and clsB did not measurably alter steady-state intracellular ion levels under standard growth conditions. Together, these results define related but non-redundant roles for two cardiolipin synthase family proteins in a common member of the human gut microbiota.IMPORTANCEThe gut bacterium Bacteroides fragilis is a normal member of the human intestinal microbiota that can also bloom to high abundance in inflamed guts. To survive within the gut, B. fragilis must maintain the integrity and function of its cell membrane. In this study, we report that the two cardiolipin synthase family genes in the B. fragilis genome impact the cell's lipid profile in distinct ways and contribute differently to how B. fragilis responds to membrane stress. Our work provides insight into how a common gut bacterium adapts to conditions encountered in the intestine and improves understanding of membrane biology in this important group of gut microbes.

mSystems.title: Dynamic nutrient competition (de-)stabilizes photosymbiosis.
mSystems.abstract: Photosymbioses between heterotrophic hosts and phototrophic symbionts are critical to productivity in oligotrophic aquatic ecosystems. The ecological success of this relationship is rooted in the efficient metabolic exchange between symbiotic partners, yet this nutritional dependency may render these systems highly sensitive to anthropogenic changes. Recent studies suggest that competitive partitioning of nutrients between partners is critical for the maintenance and regulation of symbiotic interactions. However, a solid theoretical foundation for the nutritional regulation of photosymbioses is still lacking. Thus, we designed a mechanistic population model to investigate whether observed ecological dynamics of photosymbioses can be explained by competition for the same limiting nutrient within the holobiont. Our model gives rise to a bistable system where a disturbance in nutrient competition can shift the symbiosis from a "symbiotic" state of efficient carbon recycling between the two partners into a "dysbiotic" state where no photosynthates are allocated to the host. We show that environmental factors such as temperature and nutrient availability, as well as symbiont traits such as nutrient-assimilation rates, may affect the sensitivity of the system to such disturbances. Critically, this nutritional regulation results in a trade-off in which the traits that enhance the fitness of symbiotic partners under stable conditions also enhance their susceptibility to environmental change. The model results reveal that nutrient competition is sufficient to explain ecological dynamics of establishment and initial breakdown of the symbiosis, and provide key insights into an evolutionary trajectory that favors productivity over heat resistance.IMPORTANCEPhotosymbiosis, the partnership between heterotrophic hosts and phototrophic symbionts, is a cornerstone of evolutionary innovation that sustains biodiversity from tropical coral reefs to temperate lakes. Despite their evolutionary success, these associations are surprisingly susceptible to anthropogenic change. By developing a universal population growth model, we demonstrate that the very metabolic interactions that sustain their immense productivity also create an inherent sensitivity to anthropogenic stress. We show that the competition for essential nutrients within the partnership makes the most productive symbioses the most vulnerable to breakdown. This work provides a mechanistic framework to predict how global change threatens the stability of these vital ecological cornerstones, offering a new lens through which to understand and mitigate symbiotic collapse.

mSystems.title: FNR/ArcA-2,3-butanediol regulatory axis enhances glucose uptake and adhE expression in high alcohol-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae.
mSystems.abstract: Previously, we found that Klebsiella pneumoniae is a high-alcohol producer, which contributes to the development of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its high-alcohol production remain unclear. By comparing biological phenotypes of K. pneumoniae with those of Escherichia coli, we found that the former is better at metabolizing high concentrations of glucose, exhibits faster growth rates, and produces higher levels of alcohol, with the 2,3-butanediol (2,3-BD) pathway being the key determinant underlying these differences. More importantly, species possessing the 2,3-BD pathway, including Klebsiella aerogenes, Klebsiella oxytoca, Enterobacter cloacae, and Enterobacter hormaechei, have all demonstrated high-alcohol production capabilities similar to that of K. pneumoniae, suggesting a conserved mechanism for alcohol production among 2,3-BD-positive Enterobacteriaceae. Deletion of the 2,3-BD pathway reduced the expression of the phosphotransferase system (PTS) and the alcohol dehydrogenase gene adhE, which normally confer enhanced glucose metabolism and alcohol production. Pathway deletion also downregulated multiple virulence determinants, including capsular polysaccharides (CPS), lipopolysaccharides (LPS), and type 1 and 3 fimbriae, thereby attenuating virulence in a murine pneumonia model. In addition, the regulator FNR enhanced alcohol production by upregulating adhE and 2,3-BD pathway genes, whereas ArcA activated the 2,3-BD pathway in an ArcB-independent manner, revealing a non-canonical signaling mechanism that couples metabolic adaptation with virulence. Collectively, our findings identify the "FNR/ArcA-2,3-BD pathway axis" as a key molecular mechanism driving high alcohol production in K. pneumoniae, highlighting the 2,3-BD pathway as a key link between bacterial metabolism and virulence and a potential therapeutic target for controlling K. pneumoniae infections.IMPORTANCEKlebsiella pneumoniae has emerged as a novel cause of NAFLD due to its high alcohol-producing capacity. However, the molecular basis of this phenotype remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrate that the FNR/ArcA-2,3-BD pathway axis drives high levels of alcohol production by enhancing glucose-PTS system and adhE expression, and that this pathway is conserved among Enterobacteriaceae with strong alcohol-producing abilities. Moreover, loss of the 2,3-BD pathway reduces the expression of multiple virulence factors and attenuates pathogenicity in a murine pneumonia model. These findings identify the FNR/ArcA-2,3-BD axis as a potential target for mitigating excessive alcohol production and virulence in bacteria.

mSystems.title: Environmental gradients shape the hydrocarbon-degrading microbiome in two mid-Atlantic bays.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Hydrocarbons are recalcitrant organic matter that is released into the environment via natural and anthropogenic activities. We hypothesized that abiotic and biotic factors, including salinity, temperature, seasonality, microbial interactions, and functional redundancy, influence the abundance and activity of potential hydrocarbon degraders in the Delaware and Chesapeake Bays. We identified key genes in hydrocarbon degradation pathways in metagenomes, metatranscriptomes, and metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from these estuaries. In the surface waters of both estuaries, aerobic aromatic and alkane degradation pathways predominated, with higher gene abundances observed in low-salinity spring and summer samples. Salinity significantly structured both hydrocarbon-degrading MAG abundances, alongside temperature, nitrate, and silicate concentrations, and hydrocarbon degradation gene expression, which additionally varied seasonally, with the highest relative expression of aromatic degradation genes in low-salinity samples. Catechol degradation pathways exhibited high functional redundancy, whereas the naphthalene degradation pathway showed restricted distribution. Co-expression analysis revealed that Burkholderiales displayed condition-dependent metabolic coupling, while Pseudomonadales integrated hydrocarbon degradation with fermentation and central metabolism, demonstrating complementary strategies that support multi-scale ecosystem resilience. Together, these results support our hypothesis that environmental gradients and taxon-specific metabolic strategies jointly structure the abundance and in situ activity of hydrocarbon degraders, with implications for predicting ecosystem responses to hydrocarbon inputs under changing conditions. [IMPORTANCE] Coastal estuaries are among the most contaminated aquatic environments on Earth, receiving continuous hydrocarbon inputs from industrial activity, urban runoff, and natural sources. Microorganisms are the primary agents of hydrocarbon breakdown in these systems, yet predicting when and where this capacity is active and how resilient it is to environmental change remains a major challenge. Using paired genomic and transcriptomic data from microbial genomes across two major mid-Atlantic estuaries, we show that hydrocarbon degradation capacity is not uniformly distributed but is instead shaped by salinity, nutrients, and seasonality in pathway-specific ways. Critically, dominant degrader taxa employ fundamentally different metabolic strategies to sustain this function across fluctuating conditions, providing a form of community-level insurance against environmental disturbance. These findings advance our ability to predict microbial hydrocarbon degradation in coastal systems and inform nature-based approaches to bioremediation under increasing climate and anthropogenic pressures.

mSystems.title: Analysis of metabolic interactions in an artificial consortium including butyrogenic gut microbes.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Cross-feeding interactions shape gut microbial communities and contribute to the establishment of bacteria associated with beneficial fermentation products such as butyrate. However, many gut microbes involved in fiber degradation and butyrate-associated trophic networks remain poorly characterized. Here, we combined genomic analysis of candidate strains, genome-scale metabolic modeling, in vitro cultivation, and transcriptomics to investigate metabolic interactions among gut bacteria during growth on inulin. Genomic analyses identified genes associated with inulin utilization, fermentation enzymes, and amino acid synthesis and transport. In vitro screening of different bacterial combinations on inulin identified Clostridium sp. HGF2 as an inulin-degrading, butyrate-producing strain, leading us to focus on its interaction with Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis PT33. Co-culture assays, transwell experiments, and batch bioreactor analyses supported metabolic interactions between both strains during growth on inulin. Although PT33 did not enhance butyrate production, the combined results were consistent with competition for readily available carbohydrates, while transcriptomics and model integration suggested that HGF2 degrades inulin and releases simple carbohydrates that can be utilized by PT33, while PT33 produces acetate and lactate that support HGF2 metabolism. Altogether, this work shows a methodology to identify and evaluate candidate cross-feeding interactions in artificial gut communities, in this case, revealing a competitive rather than synergistic interaction, and characterizes HGF2, identified here as Clostridium innocuum, as an understudied butyrate-producing, inulin-degrading strain. [IMPORTANCE] Understanding microbial and metabolic interactions that support butyrate producers is important for developing strategies to promote beneficial gut bacteria. However, most cross-feeding studies have focused on butyrate producers from the genera Faecalibacterium, Eubacterium, Anaerostipes, and Roseburia, leaving many other butyrate-producing bacteria poorly characterized. Here, we characterize the interaction between Clostridium sp. HGF2 and Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis PT33 using RNA-seq and genome-scale metabolic modeling. Starting from a pool of candidate butyrate producers selected through genomic analysis and in vitro experiments, we identified HGF2 as a strain of interest and explored its metabolic interaction with PT33.

mSystems.title: Acquisition of a toxin-antitoxin system within a mobile genetic element likely enhances Mycobacterium abscessus fitness by enforcing cargo retention.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Infections caused by the emerging pathogen Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) require prolonged multidrug treatment regimens that frequently fail because its accessory genome has incorporated a daunting array of poorly defined resistance mechanisms. However, the processes governing acquisition and retention of new genetic material within the Mab accessory genome remain poorly understood. Here, we first identified two Mab clinical strains that harbor the same uncharacterized toxin-antitoxin (TA) system at different genomic positions. Using computational analyses of the surrounding DNA context, we discovered that each TA system resides within identical mobile genetic element (MGE) cassettes whose positions exchange between the two strains via site-specific recombinases. We then applied a specialized 5' RNA-seq approach to identify initiator tRNAfMet as the exclusive RNA target of the VapC2 TA toxin residing within the MGE. VapC2-mediated tRNAfMet inactivation by cleavage at its anticodon stem loop leads to growth arrest and global translation inhibition. This activity ensures stable inheritance of the MGE and its resident cargo genes through a mechanism similar to postsegregational killing. Our findings uncover the mechanism for durable expansion of the Mab accessory genome and suggest a selective advantage whereby toxin-mediated entry into a reversible growth-arrested state may reduce antibiotic susceptibility. Together, these results illustrate how retention of horizontally acquired MGEs containing a potent TA system can drive adaptive genome evolution to enhance fitness in this highly drug-resistant pathogen. [IMPORTANCE] Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) causes chronic lung disease and skin and soft tissue infections, posing a major threat to individuals with cystic fibrosis, underlying lung disease, lung transplants, or weakened immune systems. Unlike Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mab has a large and highly plastic accessory genome generally thought to be predominantly shaped by horizontal gene transfer and recombination. However, the mechanisms that stabilize newly acquired genetic material in this pathogen remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a toxin-antitoxin (TA) system embedded within a mobile genetic element (MGE) predicted to enforce stable retention of the MGE through a mechanism similar to postsegregational killing. The toxin inactivates initiator tRNAfMet, inducing reversible growth arrest that likely reduces antibiotic efficacy. By functioning as an addiction module, this TA system also ensures stable inheritance of co-transferred accessory genes within the MGE, providing a mechanism for long-term retention of horizontally acquired genetic material that enhances pathogen fitness.

mSystems.title: Capture sequencing enables enhanced genome recovery of Borrelia burgdorferi in mice.
mSystems.abstract: The Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi, maintains a low burden during vertebrate infection. This limitation has historically proven to be particularly challenging for genome-based studies of B. burgdorferi infection and spirochete presence after antibiotic treatment. Here, we used TBDCapSeq, an oligo capture-based next- generation sequencing assay, to demonstrate its utility for genome recovery of B. burgdorferi directly from C3H- and BALB/c-infected mice. Tissue fragments from the ear, heart, tarsus, and infection-site skin were collected at 3 and 6 months post-tick infection from antibiotic-treated and untreated animals. We evaluated 59 tissues from 20 untreated mice and 48 tissues from 17 doxycycline-treated mice for spirochete burden and extent of genome recovery. In the untreated mice, genome recovery from each tissue was determined by the amount of borrelial DNA present in the sequencing library and was highest in the ear and heart, followed by the skin, and lowest in the tarsus. We established that approximately 50% of the genome could be recovered with as few as 10 spirochetes per assay and >90% recovery could be achieved with only 35 spirochete genomes. In the antibiotic-treated mice, trace quantities of fragmented Borrelia DNA were still present in tissues at 3 and 6 months. However, none of the tissue samples from these mice yielded an intact B. burgdorferi genome characteristic of a viable spirochete. Combined, our findings demonstrate that capture sequencing enables genomic analyses of B. burgdorferi directly within animal hosts.IMPORTANCELyme disease, caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, is the most common tick-borne infection in the United States. Low pathogen burden is a major limitation of B. burgdorferi studies in animal hosts and humans that has impacted a wide range of studies ranging from diagnostics, evolutionary analyses, and pathogenesis. It has also contributed to the controversies regarding B. burgdorferi persistence after antibiotic treatment. We show that a next-generation capture sequencing-based approach can readily overcome the current limitations of B. burgdorferi genomic analyses within animal hosts. We successfully recovered abundant genomic information directly from mouse tissues, and we did not find genetic evidence of intact bacteria present after antibiotic treatment. This approach can be employed to gain further insights into B. burgdorferi and provide critical genome data during animal and human infection.

mSystems.title: Comparative transcriptional network analysis reveals ecological specialization in infant-associated species of Bifidobacterium.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Bifidobacterium species are important microorganisms in the infant gut microbiota displaying substantial genomic diversity, yet how this variability is reflected in transcriptional regulatory architecture remains an open question. Here, we integrated pangenome analysis with transcription factor binding site inference and network-based approaches to compare regulatory architectures across Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis, Bifidobacterium breve, and B. longum subsp. longum using over 300 high-quality genomes. All three species exhibited open pangenomes, with regulatory interactions frequently involving accessory genes. Inferred network metrics were compared with score-randomized controls across motif-score thresholds. Increasing score stringency reduced network size while increasing the number of detected communities, indicating greater fragmentation of the retained networks rather than a measured increase in modularity. NrdR showed an intermediate overlap in the Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COG) category sets represented among its predicted targets and species-dependent target prevalence. HMO-related regulators (FucR, NanR, and NagR) differed descriptively between Bifidobacterium infantis and B. breve, the two species included in the complete three-regulator comparison, in predicted target counts, represented COG category sets, and genomic-prevalence patterns; only FucR showed a significant difference in accessory-target fraction. These findings identify species-dependent differences in predicted regulon composition and genomic prevalence and provide testable hypotheses about how regulatory architecture may relate to ecological specialization in the infant gut. [IMPORTANCE] Bifidobacterium species are among the most abundant microorganisms in the breast-fed infant gut microbiota, where they display distinct patterns of genomic diversification and host association. However, the transcriptional regulatory mechanisms underlying these species-specific differences remain incompletely characterized. Here, we reconstructed and compared genome-scale transcriptional regulatory networks across three infant-associated Bifidobacterium species, integrating pangenome structure with transcription factor binding site inference across more than 300 genomes. Our analyses identified predicted regulatory interactions involving accessory genes and species-specific differences in network structure, regulon composition, and target prevalence. These associations provide hypotheses for experimental studies of how gene content and regulatory architecture may contribute to niche adaptation. This pangenome-scale framework can support the prioritization of regulatory hypotheses for future functional studies of infant-associated Bifidobacterium.

mSystems.title: Association of quantitative sputum Candida load with respiratory dysbiosis and airway inflammation in suspected invasive pulmonary candidiasis.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The clinical significance of Candida species isolation from sputum remains ambiguous due to the colonization-infection dilemma. Integrating quantitative culture with microbiome profiling may clarify its role, yet systematic evidence is scarce. In this exploratory study (June 2023-June 2026), we enrolled 140 hospitalized patients suspected of invasive pulmonary candidiasis (IPC) and stratified them into possible IPC (n = 36), probable IPC (n = 71), and negative control (n = 33) groups based on clinical criteria. All underwent quantitative fungal culture of sputum and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). Patients were stratified by sputum Candida species load into low (<105 CFU/mL), high (≥105 CFU/mL), and negative control (0 CFU/mL) groups. We investigated associations between Candida species burden, respiratory microbiota, local inflammation (IL-8), and clinical outcomes. Higher Candida species load was significantly associated with prolonged hospitalization, elevated sputum IL-8, an increased microbial dysbiosis index, and depletion of key commensals (e.g., Neisseria, Prevotella, Rothia, Streptococcus, and Veillonella). Counterintuitively, it correlated negatively with several classic bacterial pathogens (such as Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa). A random forest model identified a nine-species microbiome signature that effectively discriminated probable from possible IPC (AUC, 0.877; 95% CI, 0.662-0.944). In patients with suspected IPC, higher sputum Candida species load is associated with exacerbated respiratory dysbiosis and airway inflammation. Quantitative Candida species assessment combined with microbiome signatures may serve as a complementary tool for stratifying disease severity and ecological disruption, meriting further validation in larger, multicenter cohorts. [IMPORTANCE] Respiratory specimens dominate clinical fungal cultures, yet interpreting the role of Candida spp. in sputum remains a diagnostic dilemma. Here, by integrating quantitative culture with metagenomic sequencing, we show that a high sputum Candida species load is a marker of profound ecological disruption. High Candida species burden was associated with significant depletion of key commensals, an elevated dysbiosis index, and heightened local inflammation. Counterintuitively, it correlated negatively with several classic bacterial pathogens, revealing a distinct dysbiotic signature. Moreover, a microbiome-based model accurately discriminated patients with probable invasive pulmonary candidiasis. Our findings suggest that quantitative sputum Candida species load, interpreted within the context of the microbial community, may be a practical biomarker for identifying patients with significant respiratory dysbiosis and inflammation, offering a path toward more refined, ecology-informed therapeutic strategies.

mSystems.title: A global atlas of the gut virome reveals subtype-specific and functional alterations in irritable bowel syndrome.
mSystems.abstract: The gut virome is a critical component of the microbiome-gut-brain axis; however, its role in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) remains poorly understood due to limited sample sizes and geographic bias. We aimed to construct a comprehensive global atlas of the IBS gut virome to elucidate its composition, functional potential, and clinical relevance across diverse populations and IBS subtypes. We integrated multi-cohort data comprising 1,104 samples (790 IBS patients and 314 healthy controls) from 11 cohorts across 10 geographic regions. A standardized bioinformatic pipeline was employed to perform viral mining from metagenomic and virus-like particle-enriched metaviromic data. The IBS virome exhibited significant taxonomic alterations, with specific viral signatures distinguishing IBS-D, IBS-C, and IBS-M subtypes. Geographic region was identified as a significant factor influencing the viral community structure. Functionally, the IBS virome was enriched in auxiliary metabolic genes involved in carbon metabolism and neurotransmitter precursor synthesis (histidine and tryptophan metabolism), as well as a distinct profile of virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes. Furthermore, in a specific cohort, certain viral taxa were significantly correlated with the severity of anxiety and depression. Machine learning models based on viral signatures achieved robust performance for IBS subtyping (area under the curve = 0.92). This study establishes a global baseline for the IBS gut virome, demonstrating that viral communities are dynamically shaped by geography and disease subtypes while encoding gene repertoires with the potential to influence host physiology, thereby providing a foundational resource for precision medicine.IMPORTANCEResearch on the human gut microbiome in IBS has focused primarily on bacteria, leaving the viral component as a vast and poorly understood reservoir. By profiling over 1,000 human samples globally, this study characterizes the taxonomic and functional features of the IBS gut virome. We demonstrate that these viral communities vary across geographic populations and IBS subtypes and are enriched in specific auxiliary metabolic genes, virulence factors, and antibiotic resistance genes. In addition, certain viral profiles show significant correlations with patient psychological symptoms such as anxiety and depression. This study also evaluates the potential of virome-based diagnostic biomarkers. Consequently, our findings provide a valuable reference for future in-depth research into the specific roles and mechanistic contributions of the gut virome in the pathogenesis of IBS.

mSystems.title: Multi-omics elucidate octapeptin mechanisms in alleviating intestinal injury in mice challenged with ETEC K88 via modulated microbial and host pathways.
mSystems.abstract: The mechanisms whereby antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) confer intestinal protection during enteric bacterial infection remain unclear. Here, we examined the protective effects and underlying mechanisms of the AMP, octapeptin, against intestinal infection induced by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli K88 (ETEC K88) in mice. Octapeptin ameliorated intestinal injury by modulating gut microbiome-host interactions. When compared with ETEC K88 mice, octapeptin significantly attenuated growth retardation, systemic oxidative stress, pro-inflammatory cytokine elevation, and ileal morphological damage. Integrated cecal microbiome, metabolome, and ileal transcriptome analyses revealed that octapeptin reversed ETEC K88-induced dysbiosis, notably increasing beneficial genera abundance. Concomitantly, octapeptin altered microbial metabolite profiles and significantly influenced ileal gene expression in circadian rhythm regulation. Correlation analysis and variance partitioning further identified a coherent "microbiota-metabolite-transcriptome" axis underlying these phenotypic improvements. Thus, octapeptin alleviates ETEC K88-induced intestinal injury via multi-level interactions that restore microbial ecology and regulate host circadian and immune pathways, thereby highlighting host-directed AMP mechanisms.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial peptides are promising alternatives to antibiotics, but how they work inside the body remains poorly understood. Using a multi-omics approach, this study shows that octapeptin, a natural cyclic lipopeptide, protects mice against intestinal infection by reshaping the gut microbiota, reprogramming gut metabolites, and stabilizing host circadian clock genes that are disrupted by infection. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between gut microbes and the intestinal circadian clock. This mechanistic framework could guide the development of peptide-based strategies to prevent enteric infections in animals.

mSystems.title: Comparative performance of reference-based metagenomic tools to identify species-level taxa among families of bacteria: benchmarking Mycobacteriaceae and Neisseriaceae.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Hypotheses concerning the ecology and evolution of bacteria commonly relate to the presence and abundance of species in various settings and conditions. Shotgun metagenomics may address these hypotheses, which previously relied on PCR or culture. However, the problem of determining the presence/absence of a given species of interest is not trivial, particularly when closely related species are present in the reference database or metagenomic sample. Reference-based methods for detecting species-level taxa mostly rely on thresholding of aligned reads or mapped k-mers, or derivative metrics such as genomic coverage, creating a trade-off between recall/completeness and precision/purity. New methods for species-level profiling (YACHT, Metapresence, and sylph) have recently been published. Here, we test the performance of these methods, along with Kraken2/bracken and MetaPhlAn4, to detect related species of interest using simulated metagenomic samples from genomes in the families Mycobacteriaceae and Neisseriaceae, which contain closely related genomes. Among methods tested, Metapresence, when used with an alignment quality filter, and sylph offer the best overall performance. Sylph maintains high precision but requires a depth of coverage greater than approximately 0.1× to reliably detect a genome's presence. Metapresence has a lower limit of detection of hundreds of reads, but this is balanced against relatively lower precision. Both methods are relatively robust to the presence of reads from genomes outside the groups of interest. We demonstrate the application of these methods in two real-world data sets: a mycobacterial community in a drinking water system and the community of Neisseriaceae present in the human oral cavity. [IMPORTANCE] Detecting which bacterial species of interest are present in a given sample is fundamental to studies of microbial ecology and evolution and to applied microbiology (e.g., clinical diagnostics). Culture-dependent and culture-independent (e.g., PCR) approaches are increasingly complemented by metagenomic approaches, but methods to accurately identify specific low-abundance species-level genomes in a shotgun metagenomic sample are still being refined. Here, we comprehensively test YACHT, Kraken2/bracken, Metapresence, MetaPhlAn4, and sylph using two simulated data sets of bacterial families, Mycobacteriaceae and Neisseriaceae, that contain closely related species. Our simulations exploit natural genomic diversity to create a challenging benchmark. We demonstrate that Metapresence and sylph perform best, with the former being well suited to low-biomass host-associated data sets and the latter with environmental metagenomic samples. This study is the first extensive benchmark of these methods for this use case and demonstrates that these methods can accurately identify closely related species of interest.

mSystems.title: Integrated multi-omics and metabolic modeling links structure to function in high-performing electrosynthetic biofilm communities.
mSystems.abstract: Microbial electrosynthesis (MES) is a promising technology for the valorization of CO2 into industrially relevant building blocks. The high-performing MES systems in terms of production rates of acetate (12.5-19.7 mmol L-1catholyte day-1), butyrate (1.9-12.2 mmol L-1catholyte day-1), and caproate (0.6-0.9 mmol L-1catholyte day-1) discussed in this study consist of mixed microbial communities. However, the microbial community members, metabolic pathways, and interactions driving product formation in MES communities remain poorly understood. To overcome these challenges, we conducted a comprehensive characterization of three high-performing MES communities, combining multi-omics with metagenome-scale metabolic modeling.
