Using a high-resolution metagenomic pipeline, we reconstructed high-quality genomes of 25 metagenome-assembled genomes present in our reactors, including six fully circular genomes. We report the presence of Clostridium aromativorans for the first time in a gas-fermenting system. In particular, our findings identified three acetogenic species, Eubacterium limosum, Sporomusa sphaeroides, and C. aromativorans, as key contributors to the production of acetate, butyrate, and caproate via the Wood-Ljungdahl and the reverse β-oxidation pathways. In addition, we found genes related to lactate and ethanol production from acetyl-CoA, along with proteomic evidence of lactate production. This paves the way for investigating the role of cross-fed metabolites such as lactate and ethanol as electron donors in chain elongation. Finally, meta-genome-scale metabolic modeling suggests that the communities might be sustained by the cross-feeding of specific cofactors such as pyridoxine, pantothenate, biotin, and thiamin. This study provides key insights into the structure and function of electrosynthetic communities, bringing us closer to the rational engineering of MES systems.IMPORTANCEMicrobial electrosynthesis (MES) offers a promising route to transform CO2 and renewable electricity into valuable platform chemicals. However, the microbial ecology governing the assembly and function of these systems remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to engineer them. By integrating high-resolution multi-omics with metabolic modeling, this study provides a systems-level framework to dissect the structure and function of electrosynthetic microbial communities. Understanding which organisms drive carbon fixation and chain elongation, how electrons and intermediates are transferred within the biofilm, and how metabolic dependencies structure these communities is essential for improving productivity and product specificity in MES. More broadly, this work highlights how integrated multi-omics approaches can resolve the functional organization of complex microbial ecosystems and provides methodological advances that are broadly applicable to the study and engineering of microbial communities in autotrophic, electricity-driven biotechnologies.

mSystems.title: Application of IgA-Seq in schizophrenia to identify key gut bacteria that promote abnormal behavior in mice.
mSystems.abstract: Schizophrenia (SCZ) has a complex etiology, and growing evidence implicates the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Because abundance-based profiling does not identify taxa closely engaged by mucosal immunity, we used immunoglobulin A (IgA)-based bacterial sorting to prioritize candidate SCZ-associated gut bacteria and evaluated cultured consortia in mouse models. Fecal samples were collected from participants with SCZ, other mental disorders, and healthy controls, which underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing before and after magnetic separation of IgA-coated (IgA+) and non-IgA-coated (IgA-) bacteria. Taxa prioritized by the IgA coating index were anaerobically cultured, pooled into defined IgA+ and IgA- consortia, and administered to germ-free (GF) C57BL/6J, antibiotic-pretreated Rag1-/- SPF, and conventional SPF C57BL/6J mice. In the bacterial treatment groups, MK-801 was introduced only during the final 7 days of consortium gavage; the GF NaCl control received intraperitoneal saline during the corresponding final 7-day period. Behavioral, serological, colonic, and hippocampal outcomes were assessed according to the endpoints specified for each experiment. Candidate IgA+ taxa included Streptococcus, Pseudomonas, and Parabacteroides, whereas IgA- candidates included Collinsella, Eggerthella, Bifidobacterium, Bacteroides, Enterococcus, and Clostridium. In experiment 1, the GF IgA+ and GF IgA- groups differed in open-field center-zone time (P = 0.032). Marble-burying behavior showed a significant overall difference among the five groups (P = 0.040), with a significant pairwise difference between GF IgA+ and GF IgA- mice (P = 0.022). Y-maze spontaneous alternation showed no overall group difference (P = 0.81). Forced-swim immobility showed a significant overall group effect (P = 0.020), with significant pairwise differences between GF IgA+ and GF IgA- mice (P = 0.020) and between GF IgA- and Rag1-/- IgA- mice (P = 0.030). IL-6 was frequently undetectable and was not compared statistically; TNF-α showed a significant overall analysis of variance group effect (P = 0.040), but no Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparison was significant. Colon length also showed a significant overall group effect (P = 0.010), with shorter colons in the GF IgA+ group than in the GF saline and GF IgA- groups (both pairwise P = 0.016), although colonic histology was largely normal. Descriptive hippocampal alterations were observed in GF IgA+ consortium mice. In conventional specific pathogen-free mice, MK-801 was introduced after the first 7 days of consortium gavage and continued during the final 7 days; under this exposure schedule, the IgA+ consortium was associated with greater colonic mucosal injury than the IgA- consortium. IgA-based prioritization identified candidate SCZ-associated taxa, and the resulting consortia were associated with distinct, context-dependent host responses. Individual-taxon causality remains unproven and requires validation in larger cohorts and rigorously matched animal studies.IMPORTANCESchizophrenia (SCZ) is a severe psychiatric disorder with incompletely understood biological mechanisms. Although gut microbial alterations have been reported in SCZ, abundance alone does not show which bacteria are most closely recognized by the intestinal immune system. Here, IgA-based sorting was used to prioritize immune-targeted bacterial taxa, and cultured IgA+ and IgA- consortia were evaluated in mouse experiments. The two consortia were associated with different behavioral and tissue outcomes under specific experimental conditions. In both animal experiments, bacterial gavage preceded MK-801, which was introduced during the final 7 days of gavage as a late pharmacological challenge. These findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for studying mucosal immune-microbiota interactions in SCZ, but they do not support diagnostic, therapeutic, or strain-specific causal claims.

mSystems.title: Escherichia coli-derived enterobactin is associated with delayed gut microbiome maturation in infants born to mothers with obesity.
mSystems.abstract: Maternal obesity has been increasingly recognized as a factor influencing early-life microbiome development. However, its impact on the infant gut resistome and virulome remains insufficiently characterized. In this prospective longitudinal study, we investigated gut microbiome composition, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and virulence factor profiles in infants born to mothers with obesity and normal weight during the first year of life. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed on maternal and infant fecal samples collected at birth and at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months. Infants born to obese mothers exhibited delayed microbiome maturation characterized by early enrichment of Pseudomonadota, particularly Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and reduced abundance of Bifidobacterium species. This compositional pattern was accompanied by a significantly higher ARG burden in early life, including enrichment of genes associated with antibiotic inactivation, efflux mechanisms, and β-lactam resistance. Although taxonomic differences between groups were no longer statistically detectable at the 12-month time point, where the sample size was smallest, functional disparities in the resistome persisted. Additionally, infants born to obese mothers demonstrated increased relative abundance of secretory virulence-associated genes and E. coli-derived enterobactin, suggesting enhanced iron-scavenging capacity and competitive potential of Enterobacteriaceae. Together, these findings suggest that maternal obesity is associated with altered early microbial ecological dynamics, promotes resistome expansion, and may delay transition toward a stable Bacteroidota- and Bacillota-dominated microbiome.IMPORTANCEThe first year of life is a critical window for gut microbiome development, during which early microbial disturbances may influence later health. This study shows that maternal obesity is associated not only with altered infant microbial succession but also with functional changes in the infant gut microbiome, including greater antibiotic resistance gene burden and enrichment of virulence-associated traits. The finding of increased Escherichia coli-derived enterobactin suggests that iron-scavenging mechanisms may help Enterobacteriaceae persist during early infancy and may contribute to delayed microbial maturation. By linking maternal obesity with infant microbiome development, resistome expansion, and virulence-related functions, this work provides new insight into how maternal metabolic status may shape early microbial ecology and potential microbiome-associated risks.

mSystems.title: Gut microbiota-derived indole-3-propionic acid preserves dorsal hippocampal catecholamines to prevent post-stroke cognitive impairment.
mSystems.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Gut dysbiosis has been increasingly implicated in post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI); however, the causal contribution and therapeutic potential of gut microbiota-derived metabolites remain unclear. This study aimed to identify key microbiota-derived metabolites involved in PSCI and elucidate their underlying mechanisms. We found that both PSCI patients and middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mice exhibited distinct gut microbial alterations, characterized by a marked reduction in tryptophan-metabolizing bacteria and indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), a gut microbiota-derived tryptophan metabolite. Exogenous IPA administration alleviated PSCI-like phenotypes in MCAO mice. Mechanistically, IPA preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (Th+) fibers and catecholamine levels in the dorsal hippocampus. Further analyses showed that IPA binds to the adaptor protein Ywhab, promotes ERK activation, and enhances neuronal survival, thereby counteracting neuronal apoptosis-associated inflammation, and subsequent Th+ fiber degeneration. These findings identify IPA as a gut microbiota-derived neuromodulator that mitigates PSCI by preserving dorsal hippocampal catecholaminergic transmission. IPA may therefore serve as a therapeutic candidate for PSCI. [IMPORTANCE] The advance of the present work lies in defining a mechanistic link between microbiota-derived IPA deficiency and post-stroke cognitive dysfunction rather than acute ischemic injury alone. We show that circulating IPA is persistently reduced in patients who develop PSCI and in MCAO mice and that early IPA supplementation improves post-stroke memory by preserving dorsal hippocampal TH-positive fibers and catecholamine availability. Mechanistically, we identify Ywhab as an IPA-binding protein and demonstrate that modulation of the Ywhab-ERK pathway promotes neuronal survival, limits secondary neuroinflammation, and preserves catecholaminergic projections. Importantly, Ywhab knockdown reproduced several protective effects of IPA, including reduced neuronal apoptosis and microglial activation, preservation of TH-positive fibers, and improved cognitive performance. These findings nominate Ywhab as a potential therapeutic target for PSCI and distinguish the present study from previous reports describing only the general neuroprotective effects of IPA.

mSystems.title: Population diversity and accelerated mutation drive anaerobic bacterial adaptation during long-term solvent stress.
mSystems.abstract: Experimental evolution can uncover general mechanisms by which microorganisms adapt to environmental stress. Here, we investigate evolutionary trajectories of the anaerobic, lignocellulose-fermenting bacterium Lachnoclostridium phytofermentans ISDg (family Lachnospiraceae) during >2,000 generations of automated, log-phase selection at progressively increasing butanol concentrations. Evolved clones showed large gains in fitness, reaching threefold-faster growth rates in standard medium, and robust growth at concentrations of butanol and other alcohols inhibitory to the parental strain. Longitudinal genome sequencing revealed the succession of genetic changes, including expansion of ISL3 insertion sequences, activation of a cryptic phosphotransferase system, and mutations leading to increased cell size and remodeling of membrane fatty acids. The fixation of a hypermutator genotype by generation 940 preceded a burst of genetic diversity and accelerated adaptation, followed by population destabilization as the mutational load accumulated. These findings provide insights into the mechanisms by which anaerobes acquire tolerance to industrially relevant stresses during adaptive laboratory evolution.IMPORTANCELong-term growth selection under controlled conditions can be applied to dissect complex, multigenic traits such as solvent tolerance. Butanol is an industrial solvent whose toxicity remains a major barrier to its efficient microbial production. We adapted Lachnoclostridium phytofermentans ISDg, a lignocellulose-fermenting, strictly anaerobic bacterium, to increasing butanol concentrations by automated cultivation with alternating periods of constant or variable butanol selection pressure. Evolved strains grew faster and tolerated solvent concentrations that completely inhibited the parental strain, attaining tolerance levels similar to those of native butanol producers. Genome analysis identified both previously recognized and novel adaptive changes, revealing how prolonged solvent tolerance arises through the interplay of mobile genetic elements, cellular restructuring, and altered mutation rates.

mSystems.title: Iron-dependent metabolic rewiring drives tryptophan-associated melanin production in a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain.
mSystems.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a human opportunistic pathogen, capable of producing a wide range of metabolites, including pyomelanin, which results from alterations in tyrosine catabolism. In contrast, melanin synthesis from tryptophan has never been reported in Pseudomonas. In this study, we applied an integrated multi-omics approach to characterize physiological adaptations associated with the emergence of a tryptophan-associated melanin-like pigment in P. aeruginosa PAH, a persistently re-isolated strain from a cystic fibrosis patient. Structural analysis revealed the production of a previously unreported melanin-like polymer produced under tryptophan supplementation, coexisting with a pyomelanin-like soluble fraction. This melanin exhibited iron-reduction capacity, supporting a potential physiological role in iron acquisition within the infective niche. Genome analysis identified mutations affecting iron acquisition, including genes involved in pyoverdine biosynthesis. Transcriptomic profiling revealed a coordinated reprogramming of iron homeostasis, characterized not only by the downregulation of pyoverdine-associated genes but also by altered expression of alternative siderophore systems and a broader set of genes, such as redox response pathways. Non-targeting metabolomic analyses uncovered the accumulation of indole-derived compounds. Inhibitors of tyrosine and tryptophan catabolism demonstrated a metabolic shift between these pathways. Notably, iron availability emerged as a key regulator of this system, with iron limitation promoting pigment production and associated metabolic states. Integrating these data sets, we developed an integrative model linking iron homeostasis, genomic variation, transcriptional and metabolic reprogramming, and melanin production in P. aeruginosa PAH. Overall, tryptophan arises as a key compound for melanin production in a Pseudomonas strain, expanding the diversity of melanins synthesized by this genus.IMPORTANCEThis study reveals a previously unrecognized way by which Pseudomonas aeruginosa can produce melanin, a protective pigment linked to survival and persistence in hostile environments. Here, we report how a novel melanin pigment, produced in tryptophan-supplemented media, can reduce iron and is linked to iron homeostasis in a clinical P. aeruginosa strain. Employing a multi-omics approach, we show that this pathway operates primarily through anthranilate and indolic intermediates and is favored under iron-limited conditions. This finding deepens current understanding about pigment diversity in bacteria and highlights the remarkable metabolic flexibility of P. aeruginosa during infection. Since the same phenotype was observed again in year-later isolates from the same patient, our results suggest a potential role of this trait in long-term infection and adaptation.

mSystems.title: Leviathan: fast, memory-efficient, and scalable taxonomic and pathway profiling for (pan)genome-resolved metagenomics and metatranscriptomics.
mSystems.abstract: Functional profiling of meta-omics is essential for understanding microbial communities, yet support for custom genome-resolved reference databases is limited. We introduce Leviathan for integrated taxonomic and functional profiling at both genome and pangenome resolution. Leviathan combines Sylph for ultrafast alignment-free taxonomic profiling with Salmon for pseudo-alignment-based read quantification in DNA space against (pan)genome-resolved gene catalogs, producing dual metrics per (pan)genome: pathway abundance and graph-based pathway coverage. Benchmarking alignment backends on synthetic metagenomes, we show that DNA-space pseudo-alignments retain competitive (pan)genome-level classification performance compared to traditional alignment, reducing resource requirements, while translated searches in protein space lose classification resolution from ambiguous mapping events. Leviathan's utility is demonstrated through two case studies: a marine plastisphere metagenomics data set analyzing metabolic shifts between early and mature biofilm communities, and a dental caries metatranscriptomics data set where co-expression network analysis identified organism-specific transcriptional patterns diagnostic of health and disease states. Leviathan is available at https://github.com/jolespin/leviathan.IMPORTANCEUnderstanding what microbes can do, not just which ones are present, is central to translating microbiome research into actionable insight. Existing functional profiling tools either rely on fixed reference databases or require complex multi-step pipelines when applied to custom genome collections, and none natively compute per-(pan)genome pathway abundance and graph-based pathway completeness in a single workflow. This limits the ability for researchers to directly compare functional profiles to tangential analyses on their specific genome catalogs. Leviathan addresses this gap with integrated taxonomic and functional profiling against user-defined (pan)genome-resolved references using pseudo-alignment, achieving competitive classification accuracy, with lower resource requirements compared to current methods. Native pangenome support enables routine quantification of metabolic potential and transcriptional activity at both genome and pangenome resolution, revealing functional variation across related strains that single-genome or community-level analyses obscure.

mSystems.title: A hyphal release-capture soil microcosm for recovering hyphosphere bacterial communities.
mSystems.abstract: Fungal hyphae form spatially confined interfaces in soil that mediate close associations with bacteria, collectively referred to as the hyphosphere. Despite its recognized ecological importance, experimental access to hyphosphere-associated microbial communities under realistic soil and plant-associated conditions has remained limited. Here, we present a soil-mimetic microcosm that enables controlled recovery of hyphosphere bacterial communities embedded within plant-associated soil. The system integrates field-derived soil, a native soil microbial inoculum, living cotton seedlings, and a spatially constrained fungal inoculum housed within sterile cell-strainer assemblies, permitting hyphal extension into soil while preserving a recoverable fungal-soil boundary. Using the soil-borne plant pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum as a model filamentous fungus, we show that the microcosm enables reproducible recovery of hypha-associated soil microaggregates containing physically attached bacterial cells. Full-length 16S rRNA profiling revealed pronounced reductions in bacterial richness and evenness in hyphosphere samples relative to bulk and rhizosphere soils (Shannon diversity, Kruskal-Wallis H = 15.25, P = 0.0016, with genus richness declining by 87% in bulk soil and 24% in rhizosphere soil contexts), consistent with recruitment of a restricted subset of the surrounding microbiota. Ordination analyses demonstrated clear compositional separation between soil and hyphosphere compartments (PERMANOVA F = 7.14, R2 = 0.572, P = 0.001), with hyphosphere communities of bulk and rhizosphere origin converging to similar composition despite differing starting soils (R2 = 0.128, P = 0.307). Phylogenetic turnover analyses (βNTI) indicated phylogenetic structuring (exceeding the +2 threshold), whereas taxonomic analyses identified a conserved set of bacterial genera consistently associated with hyphae, alongside compartment-specific taxa influenced by soil and plant context. Together, these findings establish the novel hyphal release-and-capture microcosm as a reproducible, ecologically grounded platform for studying hyphosphere-associated bacterial communities in plant-associated soils.IMPORTANCESoil fungi recruit distinct bacterial communities along their hyphae, forming a specialized microhabitat known as the hyphosphere. Despite its ecological importance, studying hyphosphere-associated bacteria under realistic plant-soil conditions has remained experimentally difficult. Here, we present a soil-mimetic hyphal release-capture microcosm that enables controlled reconstruction and recovery of bacterial communities assembled along fungal hyphae in intact plant-associated soils. Using the cotton wilt pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum, we show that fungal hyphae reproducibly recruit reduced and compositionally distinct bacterial assemblages from surrounding soils through strong deterministic selection. Because this pathogen is a regulated quarantine organism for which field inoculation is restricted, this system provides a tractable experimental platform for studying hyphosphere assembly under controlled yet ecologically relevant conditions. This approach provides new opportunities to investigate fungal-bacterial interactions, microbial community assembly, and plant-associated soil microbiomes at spatially resolved hyphal interfaces.

Trends in Microbiology.title: Plant autonomy in a function-rich microbial world
authors: Victor S. Pylro, Luiz Eduardo V. Del Bem, Daniel K. Morais
Trends in Microbiology.abstract: Plants evolved in environments where microbes already performed key ecological functions. We hypothesize that persistent access to reliable microbial functions may have shaped plant autonomy, favoring reduced investment in costly autonomous processes. We distinguish this from plant–microbe coevolution and propose predictions testable with comparative genomics, crop wild relatives, and experimental evolution.

Trends in Microbiology.title: A multipathogen view of Epstein–Barr virus pathogenesis and tumorigenesis
authors: Jiarui Tang, Ling Zhong, Lie Yuan, Di Su, Qinjian Zhao, Claude Krummenacher, Xiao Zhang
Trends in Microbiology.abstract: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 95% of the global population and contributes to multiple human cancers and autoimmune diseases. Co-infection with pathogens including Helicobacter pylori, human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, and Plasmodium falciparum can reshape host immunity and the EBV latency–lytic balance and, in some settings, promote reactivation. Collectively, these interactions may exacerbate chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, and epigenetic dysregulation to accelerate disease progression and tumor formation. Existing clinical treatments control only the active pathogens but fail to target latent EBV. Emerging strategies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) gene editing and EBV-targeted immunotherapy aim to eliminate latent viral reservoirs. This review outlines the synergistic mechanisms of EBV co-infection in oncogenesis, highlighting that further research on pathogen interactions is vital for developing better prevention and treatment options.

Nature Protocols.title: Prime editing-mediated site-specific recombination enables large-scale genome engineering in plants
Nature Protocols.abstract: Nature Protocols, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41596-026-01484-1Combinatorial use of two precise genome-engineering tools, prime editors and the Cre–lox recombinase system, allows targeted insertion of a large DNA sequence into a predefined locus in the plant genome.

Nature Protocols.title: Precise large-scale DNA manipulations in plants using engineered site-specific recombinase-based programmable chromosome engineering technology
Nature Protocols.abstract: Nature Protocols, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41596-026-01455-6Programmable chromosome engineering technology enables precise chromosomal-scale DNA manipulations, including insertions, replacements, deletions, inversions and translocations, in plants, with higher accuracy and efficiency than nonhomologous end joining-mediated approaches.

Cell.title: Paleogenomics illuminates mobility and changing lifeways in Chalcolithic Anatolia
authors: Ayça Aydoğan, Kıvılcım Başak Vural, Duygu Deniz Kazancı, Arda Sevkar, Eren Yüncü, Ekin Sağlıcan, Sevgi Yorulmaz, Merve Nur Güler, Reyhan Yaka, Ayça Küçükakdağ Doğu, Ezgi Sarmusak, Axel I. Cell.abstract: Contrary to the stark decline in the archaeological records in Chalcolithic Anatolia (c. 6000–3000 BCE), paleogenomics reveals that populations grew and/or became more mobile, suggesting changing lifeways. Genetic admixture with populations from eastern regions continued throughout this period, and early evidence of movement between Anatolia and the Eurasian Steppe appeared.

Cell.title: Evolutionary repurposing of a pore-forming toxin drives epithelial remodeling during terrestrial adaptation
authors: Daphne Siciliani, Ottavia Benedicenti, Marijan Posavi, Temiloluwa Omotade, Sara Ximena Amortegui, Benjamin J. Garcia, Ryan D. Heimroth, Yago Serra dos Santos, Caroline Stefani, Davorka Gulisija, Jian Chen, Boldizsár Vámosi, Balázs Enyedi, Christopher A. Johnston, Irene Salinas
Cell.abstract: In African lungfish, an evolutionarily repurposed pore-forming toxin, Protop-CrTX-A, switches its source of secretion from goblet cells to infiltrating granulocytes during estivation, driving epithelial remodeling associated with adaptation to terrestrial life.

Journal of Virology.title: A chicken interferon-stimulated gene screen reveals limited genes restricting influenza virus replication.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Avian influenza A virus (IAV) is a major global health threat. Not only does it cause significant economic losses to the agricultural industry, but it also presents a risk of spillover into the human population. However, several obstacles must be overcome for a successful cross-species transmission event to occur. One of these obstacles is the innate immunity of the host. While the innate immune response to IAV in humans has been well-studied, the innate immune response to IAV in birds is not as well understood. Here, we explore the interferon-induced immune response by identifying interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in chicken, quail, and duck cells, and find that they are largely species-specific. Using this data, we performed a CRISPR knockout ISG screen against two strains of IAV, the mouse-adapted PR8, and the low pathogenicity avian IAV isolate WF10. We find that for PR8, IFITM3 is the dominant restrictor of viral replication with several additional hits with modest effects, consistent with previous work in mammals. For avian WF10, IFITM3 was also a hit; however, there were two additional hits absent for PR8, the HSP70 co-chaperone protein BAG5 and the deubiquitinase OTUD4. Overall, these findings confirm the divergence of interferon-mediated immunity between species and establish a screening system that can be used to identify ISGs important for viral restriction in avian species.IMPORTANCEWild birds, especially waterfowl and shorebirds, are the primary natural reservoir for influenza A viruses. These birds can transmit IAV to domestic poultry, where the spillover risk to humans increases. Chickens are the most common species of domestic poultry worldwide and frequently infected with avian influenza viruses. Despite this, relatively little is known about how their immune system responds to influenza infection. This lack of knowledge creates a barrier to finding ways of preventing or mitigating IAV infection in chicken flocks. In this study, we characterized the interferon-induced immune response to IAV in chickens and found that only a small subset of ISGs were responsible for restricting IAV in chicken cells.

Journal of Virology.title: Multiplexed Fc array assays reveal the influence of TLR3 on the Th1-biased humoral response induced in mice following live-attenuated RVFV vaccination.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) can cause severe disease in humans and livestock. Several vaccine candidates are immunogenic and protective in pre-clinical animal models. Reported measurements of humoral immunity following vaccination typically assess antigen-specific activity, such as virus binding or neutralization, but do not consider the role of the Fc region. To address this knowledge gap, multiplexed Fc array assays were developed to characterize the Fc profile of antigen-specific antibodies following RVFV vaccination. The RVFV nucleocapsid protein (N) and glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) were conjugated to magnetic microspheres, and monoclonal antibodies were used to optimize assay conditions. Sera from vaccinated mice were incubated with the conjugated microspheres to capture antigen-specific antibodies, and then various detection reagents were used to measure the isotype of the antibodies and their ability to bind Fc receptors (FcRs) or complement (C1q). Two studies involving mice vaccinated with live-attenuated RVFV ΔNSsΔNSm or ΔNSs were used to demonstrate the utility of these assays. In WT C57BL/6 mice, both ΔNSsΔNSm and ΔNSs induced a high magnitude of IgG2c antibodies, indicative of a Th1-biased response; these antibodies also bound the four murine FcRs and C1q. However, following ΔNSs infection of a panel of innate immune knockout (KO) mice, several strains of KO mice, especially TLR3 KO, exhibited a reduced magnitude of IgG2c antibodies, demonstrating the impact of innate immunity on the Th1-biased response. Overall, the multiplexed Fc array assays performed as expected and can be applied to other RVFV vaccine platforms in the future to help inform rational vaccine design. [IMPORTANCE] There are currently no approved vaccines to prevent RVFV infection in humans. While some vaccine candidates exist, such as the live-attenuated ΔNSsΔNSm vaccine, most immunogenicity studies do not consider the contribution of the Fc region to antibody quality. In this study, multiplexed Fc array assays were developed to assess the Fc profile of antigen-specific antibodies following RVFV vaccination. These assays proved to be useful in identifying a Th1-biased response induced by RVFV ΔNSsΔNSm and ΔNSs and in identifying the contribution of innate immunity to this response. These assays can be applied to other RVFV vaccine platforms, such as mRNA and protein vaccines, to fully characterize the quality of an antibody response following vaccination.

Journal of Virology.title: Expanded comparative genomics supports labial gland disease viruses as a distinct and deeply divergent lineage within Naldaviricetes.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Labial gland disease viruses (LGDVs) are recently identified dsDNA viruses infecting ants, but their diversity, genomic coherence, and taxonomic boundaries have remained unresolved. Here, we expanded LGDV members by mining public arthropod genome assemblies and sequencing field-collected ants. Novel LGDV genomes were recovered from Pheidole selathorax, Proformica mongolica, Messor orientalis, and geographically distinct Anoplolepis gracilipes populations. Comparative genomic analyses demonstrate that LGDVs retain the conserved core genes in the order Lefavirales, class Naldaviricetes, share additional conservative genes with Apis mellifera filamentous virus and related viruses (AmFV/AmFLV), and encode an LGDV-restricted conservative gene set. Amino acid identity, conservative site, and gene neighborhood analyses support the internal coherence of LGDVs while distinguishing them from AmFV/AmFLV, which retained only partial local gene neighborhood similarities and lacked detectable genome-wide macrosynteny with LGDVs. Phylogenies inferred by protein sequences and structures were broadly congruent, showing that predicted protein structures retained complementary lineage-discriminating signal across deeply divergent naldaviricetes, and recovering LGDVs as a monophyletic sister group to AmFV/AmFLV. Molecular dating further supported a deep separation between these lineages, indicating that LGDVs and AmFV/AmFLV represent distinct, long-term divergent groups rather than recent derivatives of one another. Collectively, these findings support LGDVs as an internally coherent, deeply divergent, and ant-associated virus family in the order Lefavirales, class Naldaviricetes. [IMPORTANCE] Large dsDNA viruses within the class Naldaviricetes encompass deeply divergent lineages. The recent discovery of LGDVs suggests that these ant-associated viruses have a closer evolutionary relationship to the phylogenetically isolated honey bee-associated AmFV/AmFLV than other Naldaviricetes viruses. However, the classification status of LGDVs and AmFV/AmFLV remains to be determined. In this study, we identified five novel LGDV genomes from four different ant species. Comparative analyses of protein sequences and structures, as well as gene neighborhood and molecular dating analyses support that LGDVs belong to an internally coherent and divergent ant-associated lineage that is distinct from AmFV/AmFLV. This study expands the known diversity of ant-associated naldaviricetes. The broad congruence between sequence- and structure-informed phylogenies highlights the value of structure-informed approaches for resolving deep relationships among highly divergent large dsDNA viruses.

Journal of Virology.title: A seven-valent norovirus mRNA vaccine elicits robust humoral responses in preclinical models.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Noroviruses are a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis and impose a substantial global disease burden, particularly in children younger than 5 years and in older adults. Although multiple vaccine candidates are in preclinical and clinical development, no targeted intervention has been approved. We previously reported that a pentavalent mRNA vaccine candidate encoding VP1 proteins from genotypes GI.1, GII.2, GII.3, GII.4, and GII.6 elicited robust humoral and cellular immune responses in mice and nonhuman primates. Because recent surveillance data indicate increasing prevalence of GI.3 and GII.17, we designed mRNAs targeting these genotypes and evaluated an expanded seven-valent formulation in preclinical studies. We first compared candidate GI.3 and GII.17 strains in mice and selected vaccine components based on immunogenicity and cross-reactivity. The resulting seven-valent mRNA vaccine elicited strong humoral responses in mice and African green monkeys, including serum IgG binding to norovirus virus-like particles (VLPs) and functional antibodies that blocked VLP binding to histo-blood group antigens (HBGAs). Importantly, incorporation of GI.3 and GII.17 broadened functional coverage, whereas multivalent formulation introduced only limited evidence of immune interference. These findings support the feasibility of surveillance-guided updating of multivalent norovirus mRNA vaccines and highlight the adaptability of the mRNA platform for addressing emerging variants.IMPORTANCENorovirus is a major cause of vomiting and diarrhea worldwide, but developing a broadly protective vaccine is difficult because many genetically distinct strains circulate, and their prevalence changes over time. This study demonstrates a flexible vaccine strategy in which mRNA components can be selected and added based on disease surveillance and experimental evidence. We expanded a five-component norovirus vaccine to include GI.3 and GII.17, two increasingly important genotypes. The resulting seven-component vaccine generated strong antibody responses in mice and African green monkeys and broadened the range of virus types targeted by functional antibodies. Although additional studies are needed to determine whether these responses protect humans, the findings show how the adaptability of mRNA technology could support periodic updates of multivalent norovirus vaccines as circulating strains change.

Journal of Virology.title: Bovine myxovirus resistance protein (Mx)1, but not Mx2, mediates antiviral activity against human and avian influenza A viruses, including H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have recently infected dairy cows in the United States, raising concerns about human spillover. The antiviral roles of bovine host defense factors, including myxovirus resistance proteins (bMx1 and bMx2), remain relatively understudied. We examined bMx1/bMx2 induction in differentiated bovine cells following HPAI H5N1 infection and assessed their antiviral activity using overexpression, knockdown, and mutagenesis approaches. Both bMx1 and bMx2 were more strongly induced in mammary cells than in tracheal cells. Overexpression of bMx1, but not bMx2, significantly inhibited seasonal influenza A viruses (IAVs), low-pathogenic, and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses, including H5N1 2.3.4.4b, but not influenza B viruses. Conversely, knockdown of bMx1 resulted in enhanced IAV growth. Further, bMx1 inhibited early stages of viral replication, acting to reduce viral transcription and subsequent steps in the viral replication cycle. Known mutations that reduce human MxA (hMxA) activity also impaired bMx1 function, and mutations in the viral nucleoprotein (NP) associated with resistance to hMxA also reduced virus sensitivity to bMx1. Furthermore, phylogenetic analysis showed that a small minority (>0.03%) of avian H5N1 2.3.4.4b viruses already carry some of these NP mutations. These findings suggest that while current H5N1 viruses largely remain susceptible to bMx1, viral evolution or opportunistic reassortment could drive Mx resistance and increase pandemic risk.IMPORTANCEHighly pathogenic avian influenza viruses have spilled over into dairy cows and have been circulating on dairy farms in the United States since 2024. The innate antiviral immune responses of cows to influenza viruses have not been extensively studied. In this study, we focused on Mx proteins, a key part of the innate immune defense system toward viruses. We specifically looked at bovine Mx proteins and demonstrated antiviral activity toward different influenza viruses, including the highly pathogenic strains. We also showed that the mechanism of antiviral activity of bovine Mx1 was very similar to that of the human equivalent MxA protein. Further, we found that a small minority of these avian viruses have mutations associated with resistance to both bovine Mx1 and human MxA proteins. Overall, this work highlights the elevated pandemic risk for highly pathogenic influenza viruses through continual circulation in cows, a mammalian species in close proximity to humans.

Journal of Virology.title: Functional analysis of non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (amino acids 1831-1882) in facilitating pseudorabies virus entry via interaction with glycoproteins gH and gL.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Pseudorabies virus (PRV) is the etiological agent responsible for porcine pseudorabies, causing substantial financial losses in the global swine industry. Non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (NMHC IIA), as an actin-binding motor protein, has been recognized as a functional factor in herpesvirus entry. However, its precise mechanism in PRV invasion remains poorly defined. Our investigation demonstrated that targeted inhibition of NMHC IIA, using a specific chemical inhibitor, siRNA-mediated knockdown, C-terminus of NMHC IIA (sPRA, amino acids [aa] 1672-1981), or rabbit anti-sPRA serum, significantly decreases PRV infection in PK-15 cells in a dose-dependent manner. During the early stage of PRV infection, NMHC IIA underwent rapid and pronounced translocation from the cytoplasm to the cell surface, which is beneficial to the virus entry. The study identified that sPRA mediates PRV internalization by binding to viral glycoproteins gH and gL. Furthermore, we pinpointed the subdomain spanning aa 1831-1882 within sPRA as the critical domain for both mediating the interaction with gH/gL and facilitating viral internalization. These results advance our comprehension of the molecular pathways through which NMHC IIA supports PRV infection and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for PRV intervention. [IMPORTANCE] Pseudorabies virus (PRV), a member of the Alphaherpesvirinae subfamily, not only poses an ongoing threat to the global swine industry but also presents a potential zoonotic risk. Although the host protein NMHC IIA has been identified as a critical factor mediating virus entry, its precise molecular mechanism during PRV infection is still unclear. Herein, we demonstrated that NMHC IIA participates in PRV internalization through binding to viral glycoproteins gH and gL. Moreover, we precisely mapped the critical functional region, spanning amino acids 1831-1882 in the C-terminus of NMHC IIA, responsible for both the viral entry process and the interaction with viral proteins. These findings could deepen the understanding of the interaction mechanism between PRV and the host, and provide a promising broad-spectrum antiviral target.

Journal of Virology.title: Monitoring hCMV-specific T cell response in hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients via rapid whole blood cytokine release assay.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Human cytomegalovirus (hCMV) reactivations and disease frequently occur in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients as a consequence of the profound immunosuppression required to prevent graft rejection. Despite clear evidence of the role of hCMV-specific T cells in controlling hCMV replication, quantification of hCMV-specific T cells is not widely performed to inform the clinical management of hCMV reactivations after transplantation, largely due to the lack of a simple and reliable assay to assess hCMV-specific cellular immunity. Herein, we developed a simple and rapid whole blood IFN-γ/IL-2 release assay (CRA) that uses overlapping hCMV peptides to quantify the hCMV-specific T cell responses and validated it in the peripheral blood of 40 healthy donors and 20 HSCT patients post-transplant. We found that the CRA correlates well with classical IFN-γ ELISpot assays but demonstrates greater sensitivity in detecting hCMV-specific T cell responses in HSCT recipients. Notably, the CRA also captured dynamic changes in hCMV-specific T cell responses associated with hCMV reactivation. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the CRA is a simple and rapid method for longitudinal monitoring of hCMV-specific T cell immunity in HSCT recipients, with potential to inform clinical management of hCMV reactivations. [IMPORTANCE] Stem cell and organ transplant patients often experience human cytomegalovirus (hCMV) reactivations and disease due to the immunosuppression required to prevent graft rejection. While it is known that hCMV-specific T cells are effective in controlling hCMV replication, monitoring of these T cells after transplantations is not routinely done in clinics due to the lack of an easy and reliable assay to assess hCMV-specific T cells. Here, we developed a simple and rapid cytokine release assay to quantify hCMV-specific T cells directly in whole blood and validated it in the peripheral blood of healthy donors and hematopoietic stem cell transplant patients post-transplant. The assay correlated well with classical ELISPOT assays and captured the dynamic changes of hCMV-specific T cell responses associated with hCMV reactivation. Together with its simplicity, the assay is well suited for the longitudinal monitoring of hCMV-specific T cell immunity in transplant patients.

Journal of Virology.title: Modeling the Epstein-Barr virus lifecycle in the rabbit.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a human gammaherpesvirus that establishes a lifelong, persistent infection in greater than 90% of people worldwide. EBV has lacked an animal model that depicts the viral lifecycle in B cells and epithelial cells, allows for the investigation of immune responses, and models persistence in a host. EBV establishes a robust infection in immunosuppressed rabbits, resulting in widespread infection of the spleen and the development of splenomegaly. Within the spleen, follicle formation was altered as a result of EBV infection. Similar magnitudes of infection were observed in immunosuppressed rabbits infected with the B95-8 and Akata viral strains. In immunocompetent rabbits, spleen morphology appeared similar to that of mock-infected rabbits. Rabbits infected with B95-8 and Akata viruses developed antibody responses to the EBNA family of proteins in a comparable manner to human infection. Akata infections were more consistent in both the immunosuppressed and immunocompetent studies, whereas B95-8 infections resulted in variable magnitudes of infection and immune responses. The persistence of EBV in rabbits and whether the full lifecycle of EBV in lymphocytes can be replicated remain to be further examined. [IMPORTANCE] The human gammaherpesvirus Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 90% of the global population and is associated with lymphomas and carcinomas. EBV develops a lifelong, persistent infection in its host, avoiding immune detection by limiting the expression of its productive and latency genes. Currently, the EBV field lacks an animal model that can have persistent infection and immune responses to the virus during the course of infection. We demonstrated that rabbits mount an immune response to EBV infection over 6 months and may be a good model of persistent infection, although the viral genome remained below our limit of detection similar to humans.

Journal of Virology.title: Spacer peptide 2 inhibition of HIV-1.
Journal of Virology.abstract: HIV-1 virus assembly is organized by the precursor Gag (PrGag) protein, which, from its N-terminus to its C-terminus, is composed of the matrix (MA), capsid (CA), spacer peptide 1 (SP1), nucleocapsid (NC), spacer peptide 2 (SP2), and p6 domains. Evidence indicates that the full-length, wild-type (WT) HIV-1 envelope (Env) protein is incorporated into virus particles by virtue of interactions of plasma membrane-associated immature lattices assembled by the PrGag MA domains, but that Env proteins with cytoplasmic tail deletions (ΔCT) or truncations do not require such an interaction for virion incorporation. Remarkably, during PrGag proteolytic processing and viral maturation, the free SP2 peptide binds to MA proteins and drives the formation of a distinct mature MA lattice. This lattice maturation is necessary for efficient function of WT but not ΔCT Env proteins. Based on these observations, we tested whether ectopic expression of SP2 variants might inhibit HIV-1 by inappropriately driving the formation of mature MA lattices. We have found that the expression of a chimeric protein composed of the green fluorescent protein (GFP) and SP2 in virus-producing cells causes the assembly of defective viruses in a MA-dependent fashion. Viruses produced in the presence of GFP-SP2 had aberrant morphologies and incorporated significantly less Env, regardless of whether the Env protein was WT or CT-truncated. Our results suggest that it might be possible to develop SP2 derivatives into antivirals.IMPORTANCEThe matrix domain of the HIV-1 structural protein forms a hexagonal lattice at the plasma membranes of infected cells, and this lattice helps direct the assembly of immature virus particles. The immature matrix lattice is also instrumental in facilitating the incorporation of viral envelope proteins into virus particles. Surprisingly, when the HIV-1 protease processes the structural protein into its mature components, one of the peptides produced, spacer peptide 2, drives the reorganization of the immature matrix lattice into a mature form. This maturation step appears essential for envelope proteins to acquire their full activities. We have found that expressing a spacer peptide 2 variant in virus-producing cells results in the assembly of defective viruses. The viruses have aberrant morphologies and contain significantly less envelope protein than wild-type viruses. Our results suggest that it might be possible to develop spacer peptide 2 derivatives into antivirals.

Journal of Virology.title: Early innate immune signatures correlate with Ad26.COV2.S vaccine immunogenicity and protective efficacy.
Journal of Virology.abstract: The innate immune system is rapidly activated following antigen exposure and plays a critical role in shaping the ensuing adaptive immune responses. In this study, we performed bulk RNA sequencing and proteomic profiling in a cohort of 25 rhesus macaques following Ad26.COV2.S immunization to characterize early innate correlates of vaccine immunogenicity and protection. Our results show that innate immune activation occurred as early as day 1 post-vaccination and demonstrated a systemic enrichment of antiviral interferon pathways, cytokine signaling, and activation of innate immune cell signatures. These early transcriptomic signatures correlated positively with humoral and cellular immune responses at 6 weeks following vaccination and correlated inversely with viral loads following SARS-CoV-2 challenge. Similar correlates of immunogenicity were observed in a cohort of 25 adult healthy participants vaccinated with Ad26.COV2.S. Taken together, these findings highlight the importance of early activation of the innate immune responses following Ad26.COV2.S vaccination in shaping the protective adaptive immune response.IMPORTANCEEarly innate immune responses may shape vaccine immunogenicity and protection. We evaluated responses to Ad26.COV2.S vaccination in rhesus macaques and humans and found that day 1 innate immune signatures correlated with subsequent adaptive responses. These findings suggest that early post-vaccination immune programming influences immunogenicity and protective efficacy months later.

Journal of Virology.title: Novel roles of the Epstein-Barr virus BRRF1 protein in post-transcriptional RNA regulation.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] In lytic infection, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) proteins manipulate cellular processes in multiple ways to facilitate virion production and overcome host antiviral responses. Here, we screened a library of EBV lytic proteins for those that manipulate or localize to cellular processing bodies (PBs), known to play important roles in RNA surveillance and miRNA-mediated translational control. One EBV protein, BRRF1, was identified that partially localized to PBs, and affinity purification-mass spectrometry experiments showed that it interacted with the CCR4-NOT complex-a known component of PBs with multiple roles in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation. The CNOT9 subunit of CCR4-NOT was sufficient to bind BRRF1, and its downregulation diminished BRRF1 interaction with the CNOT1 scaffold protein, indicating its importance in mediating the CCR4-NOT interaction with BRRF1. A BRRF1 double-point mutant was generated that failed to bind CNOT9 or interact with CCR4-NOT and was used to assess the importance of the BRRF1-CCR4-NOT interaction. Luciferase reporter assays identified multiple roles for BRRF1 in post-transcriptional regulation, including polyadenylation-dependent destabilization effects and interference with miRNA function, the latter of which was dependent on BRRF1 binding to CCR4-NOT. In addition, mRNA sequencing experiments comparing cells with and without BRRF1 expression identified multiple transcripts affected by BRRF1, some of which were at least partly dependent on the BRRF1-CCR4-NOT interaction. These include Claudin 6, whose transcripts and protein were downregulated by BRRF1 expressed on its own, as well as in lytic infection. Thus, we have identified multiple roles for BRRF1 in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation, some of which involve interaction with CCR4-NOT. [IMPORTANCE] To efficiently generate virions, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) must manipulate cellular processes to optimize the environment and overcome host antiviral defenses. Through unbiased screening methods, we have identified an EBV protein (BRRF1) that localizes to cellular bodies, which play key roles in mRNA regulation, and that interacts with a cellular complex with multiple critical roles in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation. As expected from these interactions, we found that BRRF1 has multiple previously unknown roles in disrupting mRNA levels and translation. Interestingly, one of the transcripts targeted by BRRF1 is Claudin 6, which has multiple roles in cancers, leading to increased cell proliferation and invasion. Our study provides additional insight into how EBV proteins manipulate cells to promote infection and affect oncogenesis.

Journal of Virology.title: Engineering a low cytotoxicity recombinant rabies virus neurotracer via N-gene recoding.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Viral-vector-based tracers have proven invaluable for mapping neural circuits. Rabies virus (RV)-based retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracers have been widely used for depicting the input neural circuit of targeted neuronal populations. However, the cytotoxicity of the RV tracer limits its application. Here, we employed the synthetic attenuated virus engineering technology to recode the N gene of the RV SAD-B19 strain by codon pair deoptimization to generate attenuated RV tracers. The characteristics of the recoded RV tracers were tested both in vitro and in vivo. The full-length recoded N gene abolished viral rescue, whereas the partial recoded N gene supported successful viral recovery. Compared to its parent, the recoded RV trans-monosynaptic tracer exhibited lower cytotoxicity and labeled more input neurons. It can also robustly express proteins to visualize the neuronal morphology and manipulate the neural circuit activity. Collectively, our work generated a new retrograde trans-monosynaptic tool, which complements existing neural circuit tracers. [IMPORTANCE] Viral vectors play an important role across multiple fields in biomedicine. In the neuroscience community, rabies virus (RV)-based retrograde trans-monosynaptic tracers have been widely used to map the input neural circuits of targeted neuronal populations. However, the inherent cytotoxicity of RV-based tracers limits their broader application. In this study, we utilized synthetic attenuated virus engineering technology to recode the RV N gene, generating an attenuated neurotracer that will significantly benefit future neuroscience research.

Journal of Virology.title: Residues E124, K129, and R134 in eEF1A domain I promote ALV-J replication via association with reverse transcriptase.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Subgroup J avian leukosis virus (ALV-J) is an oncogenic retrovirus posing significant threats to the global poultry industry. While host factors are known to regulate retroviral reverse transcription, the specific host proteins that support this critical step in ALV infection have remained completely unknown. In this study, we confirmed that overexpression or knockdown of eEF1A significantly enhanced or suppressed ALV-J proliferation, respectively. Co-immunoprecipitation and molecular docking demonstrated an association between eEF1A and the ALV-J reverse transcriptase (RT). Furthermore, three conserved residues in eEF1A domain I, including glutamate 124 (E124), lysine 129 (K129), and arginine 134 (R134), were identified as critical for the eEF1A-RT association. Alanine substitution at these EKR residues disrupted the eEF1A-RT association, markedly impairing viral reverse transcription and infectious virion production. From the viral perspective, a conserved tryptophan (W250) in the RT thumb domain acts as the key counterpart to the eEF1A EKR motif, and its mutation similarly abolishes the association and viral replication. Notably, this eEF1A-RT association and its functional significance are conserved across ALV subgroups A, B, K, and J. Together, our work elucidates that three residues E124, K129, and R134 within domain I of eEF1A mediate the association with ALV-J RT, promoting viral replication by enhancing reverse transcription efficiency. This finding provides the first mechanistic insight into host-dependent regulation of reverse transcription in ALV infection, broadens the understanding of how retroviruses co-opt host factors to facilitate this critical process, and provides a rational basis for genome editing of eEF1A to generate broad-spectrum ALV-resistant poultry lines.IMPORTANCEAvian leukosis viruses (ALVs) cause severe economic losses to the global poultry industry, and current disease-resistant strategies targeting viral entry receptors only work for specific subgroups. This study identifies that the host protein eEF1A associates with ALV reverse transcriptase via conserved key residues to promote viral reverse transcription and replication, and this regulatory mechanism is conserved across multiple ALV subgroups. These findings provide a novel target for developing broad-spectrum ALV-resistant poultry breeds through genome editing, with important implications for poultry disease control.

Journal of Virology.title: Primer: Orbiviruses.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Orbiviruses comprise numerous species and are transmitted by insect vectors. They are non-enveloped viruses with a multilayered capsid and a segmented double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. Bluetongue virus (BTV), the prototype species of the genus Orbivirus, is a significant pathogen of livestock and is widely distributed throughout the world, causing serious periodic outbreaks with substantial economic consequences. Consequently, BTV has been extensively studied as a model orbivirus, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of its molecular epidemiology, genetics, biochemistry, structure, and replication cycle. This includes detailed insights into virus entry into host cells, synthesis of progeny viral components, assembly of new virions, and subsequent cell-to-cell transmission. This review summarizes the current literature on each of these aspects and discusses how this knowledge has been applied to develop novel vaccines against BTV and related orbiviruses. In addition, the review highlights important gaps in our understanding of virus replication within insect vectors, particularly Culicoides biting midges (gnats), at the molecular level. Addressing these gaps will provide valuable insights into orbivirus evolution, transmission, and the emergence of new viral strains.

Journal of Virology.title: Antagonism of PRDX1 and Japanese encephalitis virus via the autophagy pathway.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is a mosquito-borne zoonotic infectious agent and causes animal and human illness of the central nervous system. Japanese encephalitis virus inflicts severe harm, yet even with an approved vaccine, prevention and control remain daunting, and the molecular mechanism underlying the virus-host interplay remains incompletely understood. In this study, we found that the host peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1) protein inhibits JEV replication. PRDX1 targets nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) of JEV and mediates its degradation via the proteasome and autophagy pathways, thus inhibiting viral replication. By targeting TRAF6, an E3 ligase, the PRDX1 protein catalyzes the ubiquitination of NS1, leading to its recognition by NDP52, a cargo receptor, along with lysosomal degradation. We also found that the JEV NS3 protein can target and degrade PRDX1 to decrease the antiviral function of PRDX1, which is a tactic by which viruses confront the host. In conclusion, these findings showed that selective autophagy has dual functions in the host and JEV: it can degrade viral proteins to inhibit viral replication and host antiviral proteins to promote viral replication.IMPORTANCEJapanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is a flavivirus capable of inducing human encephalitis and dysgenesis in gestating sows. It has an extraordinary ability to hijack cellular systems and evade defenses, establishing infection and spreading it throughout the body to cause disease. During viral infection, the host initiates several antiviral responses and activates various host-restricted factors to resist viral invasion. In this study, we identified PRDX1 as a novel host restrictor that inhibits viral multiplication by binding to TRAF6 (an E3 ubiquitin ligase) and NDP52 (a cargo receptor) to degrade nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) of JEV. We also found that JEV infection can downregulate intracellular PRDX1 expression via nonstructural protein 3 (NS3), thus promoting viral replication. These results revealed that the virus-host interaction is a complex and dynamic process in which viruses restrict and compete with each other.

Journal of Virology.title: Pooled intravenous immunoglobulins exhibit broad binding and Fc-mediated activity against diverse SARS-CoV-2 variants.
Journal of Virology.abstract: During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), antibody-based therapies such as COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) emerged rapidly. However, many CCP clinical trials failed to show consistent benefits, and mAbs lost effectiveness as new SARS-CoV-2 variants emerged. These studies consistently indicated that antibody therapies are effective when given very early in disease and in patients with delayed or suppressed immune responses. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), which is pooled IgGs from thousands of donors, has been explored as an additional source of anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies to treat acutely ill patients because IVIG was shown to prevent disease and death in animal models against variants even without neutralizing activity. As antibodies can also protect via Fc-mediated activation of innate immune effector functions, in this study, we compared the qualitative and quantitative properties of CCP and IVIG to determine if IVIG might serve as a clinical therapeutic alternative to CCP. We measured SARS-CoV-2 spike (S)- and nucleocapsid (N)- specific antibody-binding titers across variants and evaluated their ability to induce antibody-dependent effector functions. We found that IVIG and CCP had comparable binding and Fc-effector activity against ancestral SARS-CoV-2. Remarkably, IVIG manufactured before the emergence of XBB.1.5, JN.1, KP.2, XEC, and XFG demonstrated strong binding and Fc-effector activity against these newer variants.IMPORTANCEDespite the availabilities of vaccines for SARS-CoV-2 for most individuals, there remain vulnerable populations for which vaccination is ineffective. As the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants has rendered many monoclonal antibody therapies ineffective, there remains a need to understand the role of polyclonal antibody therapies for SARS-CoV-2, such as COVID-19 convalescent plasma (CCP) and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). While CCP is variable and donor-dependent, IVIG is pooled from thousands of donors with a range of vaccine- and natural infection-derived antibody responses and may represent a consistent source of polyclonal antibodies. We compared high neutralizing antibody titer CCP, previously shown to be associated with reduced time to hospital discharge, with IVIG produced post-2021. We find that IVIG offers expanded antibody binding to SARS-CoV-2 variants, including those that emerged after the IVIG was collected, and enhanced induction of Fc-mediated innate immune effector functions, highlighting the potential utility of IVIG as an adjunct treatment of SARS-CoV-2.CLINICAL TRIALSThis study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT04524507.

Journal of Virology.title: No-known-vector flaviviruses exhibit diverse replication and virulence phenotypes in mice.
Journal of Virology.abstract: The Orthoflavivirus genus (flaviviruses) includes globally significant arboviruses, which cycle between arthropod vectors (mosquitoes and ticks) and vertebrate hosts. In contrast, no-known-vector flaviviruses (NKVFVs) have been isolated from rodents and bats, but not arthropods, so they are thought to spread by vector-independent routes. However, little is known about the host range and pathogenic mechanisms of these viruses. To evaluate NKVFV pathogenesis, we infected wild-type, Ifnar1-/-, and Ifnar1-/- Ifngr1-/- mice by footpad inoculation with 12 NKVFVs: Entebbe bat virus (ENTV), Sokuluk virus (SOKV), Yokose virus (YOKV), Modoc virus (MODV), Apoi virus (APOIV), Jutiapa virus (JUTV), Sal Vieja virus (SVV), Dakar bat virus (DBV), Rio Bravo virus (RBV), Montana myotis leukoencephalitis virus (MMLV), Phnom Penh bat virus (PPBV), and Tamana bat virus (TABV). We compared these NKVFVs to the mosquito-borne Zika virus and Kedougou virus and to the tick-borne Langat virus and Kadam virus. We monitored disease signs and measured viremia. Seven NKVFVs (ENTV, SOKV, YOKV, MODV, APOIV, DBV, RBV) were virulent in Ifnar1-/- mice, causing 100% lethality within 9 days post-infection, accompanied by viremia. All viruses tested were virulent in Ifnar1-/- Ifngr1-/- mice and produced greater viremia compared to Ifnar1-/- mice. No viremia or disease signs were detected in wild-type mice. We further evaluated RBV, MMLV, and PPBV replication in mouse primary fibroblasts and bone marrow-derived macrophages, as well as in cell lines from three bat species. Altogether, our results provide new information about the virulence and replication phenotypes of NKVFVs, supporting future studies investigating NKVFV-specific and pan-flavivirus pathogenic mechanisms.IMPORTANCEFlaviviruses that cause human disease are transmitted by mosquitoes and ticks (e.g., West Nile virus, yellow fever virus, tick-borne encephalitis virus). But there are related flaviviruses that are not known to infect arthropods, so are thought to spread by vector-independent routes (no-known-vector flaviviruses, NKVFVs). Not much is known about NKVFVs, but they provide an opportunity to understand flavivirus replication, tropism, and pathogenesis more broadly. We evaluated a panel of 12 NKVFVs for their ability to cause disease in mice with and without antiviral interferon responses as well as their replication in mouse cells. Our findings provide new information about these under-studied viruses and demonstrate which mouse models may be appropriate to use for further studies with NKVFVs.

Journal of Virology.title: Expanding the Orchidaceae virome through analysis of public-domain sequencing data.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Orchidaceae is one of the largest plant families and includes species of major ornamental, economic, and ecological importance. Despite this diversity, the viruses associated with orchids remain poorly characterized. The growing availability of high-throughput sequencing data offers new opportunities to explore plant virus diversity across broad taxonomic scales. Here, we conducted a large-scale meta-analysis of orchid-associated viruses by reanalyzing 2,789 publicly available RNA-seq data sets representing 41 genera across 18 subtribes and five subfamilies. We identified sequences corresponding to 163 viruses, including 13 new associations with orchids. Notably, 117 sequences likely represent putative novel species, including tentative new genera within the families Benyviridae, Betaflexiviridae, Phenuiviridae, and Tymoviridae. This analysis also reveals patterns of virus co-occurrence within the orchid virome and uncovers links between viral taxa and orchid life forms. Overall, these findings greatly broaden the known diversity of orchid-associated viruses and offer a comprehensive global framework for understanding their composition, ecological interactions, and potential scope.IMPORTANCEOrchids are among the most diverse plant families, yet little is known about the viruses associated with them. Plant viruses pose significant risks to agriculture and may also threaten orchid conservation, particularly when infected plant material is moved through trade or cultivation. A comprehensive understanding of the orchid virome is therefore essential for improving virus detection, managing diseases, and producing virus-free planting material. In this study, we used large-scale analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data to identify viral sequences associated with orchid-derived transcriptomic data sets and to characterize the diversity of orchid-associated viruses. Our results substantially expand the catalog of viruses associated with Orchidaceae, revealing numerous previously undescribed viruses and candidate virus-orchid associations. By providing a global perspective on the Orchidaceae virome, this work highlights the power of data mining approaches for virus discovery and establishes a foundation for future studies on plant virus ecology, evolution, and surveillance.

Journal of Virology.title: Characterization of norovirus GI.3 and GII.12 variants detected in wastewater: proof-of-concept for integrating phenotypic insights in wastewater-based epidemiology.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Norovirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis, responsible for 685 million cases and 200,000 deaths annually. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) enables not only global surveillance of dominant strains but also the detection of cryptic and emerging viral variants. An important question, however, is how to link genomic diversity to clinical impact and phenotypic traits of the strains detected in wastewater. In the Global Urban Wastewater Project, phylogenetically distinct norovirus GI.3 and GII.12 lineages were detected in wastewater from Cameroon. In this study, we characterized their host- and tissue-binding specificity and antigenic makeup in comparison with other GI.3 and GII.12 lineages using a luciferase immunoprecipitation system-based assay, alongside sequence analysis of the VP1 P2 subdomain. We observed intra-genotype variation among GI.3 variants. GI.3 Cameroon/2017 shared phenotypes with its closest reference strain (GI.3 Mexico/2016), and their histo-blood group antigen (HBGA)-binding profiles suggested a narrower susceptible population compared to other GI.3 lineages. Conversely, GII.12 strains showed no significant differences in HBGA binding, antigenic profiles, and tissue attachment. Together, these results reveal distinct patterns of phenotypic diversity between the two genotypes. While GI.3 variants exhibited lineage-specific traits, the GII.12 strains appeared phenotypically conserved across lineages. These findings highlight the feasibility and importance of integrating phenotypic analysis with WBE to assess potential public health risks posed by novel viral variants. [IMPORTANCE] While detection of norovirus through case-based surveillance is limited to variants causing symptomatic infection, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) allows for detection of cryptic and emerging variants. However, validation, such as phenotypic characterization, is needed to assess the clinical importance of a variant detected in WBE. In this study, we investigated the phenotypic traits of genetically distinct GI.3 and GII.12 lineages detected in wastewater from Cameroon. We utilized NanoLuc luciferase immunoprecipitation system (N-LIPS)-based assays to assess binding specificity and antigenicity. Compared to traditional methods involving virus isolation and virus-like particle production, N-LIPS-based assays are considerably less laborious and faster. This allows for rapid characterization of novel variants, making the timely assessment of phenotypic changes of such variants for outbreak or pandemic preparedness feasible. Finally, by integrating insights from phenotypic assays, we showed the possibility of expanding the public health value of wastewater surveillance in assessing the risk of novel viral variants.

Journal of Virology.title: Infection-specific long-chain fatty acid metabolism as a broad anti-enterovirus target.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Enteroviruses are arguably the most numerous group of viruses infecting humans. While most enterovirus infections are benign and self-resolving, their sheer number inevitably increases the chances of multiple complications. The diversity of enteroviruses means that the development of vaccines is only economically feasible against a select few, and no direct-acting or host-targeted anti-virals are approved to treat enteroviral infections, largely due to the rapid development of resistance against all experimental drugs. Here, we explored a universal property of enterovirus infection-a massive upregulation of phospholipid synthesis as a target for anti-viral interventions. The increased phospholipid synthesis consumes endogenously and exogenously derived long-chain fatty acids (LCFA). We demonstrate that polyunsaturated LCFAs can have a broad anti-enteroviral effect, affecting multiple steps of the virus life cycle. The anti-viral activity of LCFAs did not strictly depend on the degree of unsaturation or their capacity to induce lipid peroxidation, but significantly correlated with their conformation. This suggests that their incorporation into the phospholipid molecules makes the replication organelle membranes incapable of properly accommodating viral replication machinery. Accordingly, the inhibition of neutral lipid synthesis promoted LCFAs retargeting to the membranes in infected cells and increased their anti-viral potency. We show that this approach is effective against diverse enteroviruses in different cell types, including differentiated primary cells, and that attempts to establish viruses resistant to such treatment were unsuccessful.IMPORTANCEHumans are hosts to more than 300 distinct enteroviruses. Enterovirus infections can induce multiple short-term and long-term complications, including such serious conditions as paralysis, myocarditis, aseptic meningitis, and others. Yet, licensed vaccines are available only against poliovirus and enterovirus A71, and no specific anti-enterovirus drugs are approved for clinical practice. These viruses rapidly develop resistance to either virus- or host-acting experimental compounds. We explored a shared feature of enterovirus infection, a strong upregulation of phospholipid synthesis in infected cells, as a tool to control enterovirus replication. By altering the long-chain fatty acids composition available to infected cells, replication of diverse enteroviruses can be similarly suppressed, and the selection of resistant mutants was not successful. Thus, targeting infection-induced changes in cellular lipid metabolism, rather than individual viral or host factors, may offer a promising approach for controlling enterovirus infections.

Journal of Virology.title: Primer: Functions and evolution of viral proteins.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Viruses encode an enormous variety of proteins that jointly comprise the largest pool of protein diversity on Earth. At coarse grain, the viral pan-proteome can be partitioned into four classes of proteins that differ in their evolutionary conservation, spread across the virosphere, and broadly defined functionality: (i) viral hallmark proteins (VHPs) that are broadly conserved across different realms of viruses, (ii) proteins responsible for core viral functions, such as replication, expression, and virion structure, but are more narrowly represented within a single virus realm, kingdom, or phylum, (iii) fast-evolving proteins involved in virus-host interactions, particularly counter-defense, that are typically conserved only in narrow groups of viruses, (iv) "dark matter," that is, proteins without detectable homologs or known functions, typically shared only by closely related viruses. Apart from the few VHPs that might descend from the primordial protein pool, most of the viral proteins are derived from cellular ancestors, via recruitment of proteins with activities relevant for virus replication, and extensive exaptation. The recruitment of cellular proteins for roles in viral reproduction follows a logic dictated by the functionalities that are relevant for viruses. Thus, different groups of viruses often convergently capture distinct, sometimes unrelated proteins, providing similar activities, for example, polymerases, helicases, and proteases of different families. Recent advances in protein structure prediction and analysis provide unprecedented insights into the organization and evolution of the viral pan-proteome.

Journal of Virology.title: Primer: Giant viruses of protists.
Journal of Virology.abstract: Giant viruses infecting protists have expanded our understanding of viral diversity. These members of the phylum Nucleocytoviricota possess genomes that can exceed 2.5 Mb and encode hundreds to thousands of proteins, including functions once thought unique to cellular organisms. They infect amoebae, algae, and other unicellular eukaryotes, forming large factories and interacting with virophages and mobile genetic elements. Their virions display diverse architectures, from icosahedral particles to amphora-shaped pandoraviruses and tail-bearing tupanviruses. Comparative genomics highlights evolutionary processes such as horizontal gene transfer, gene duplication, de novo gene birth, and genome rearrangements, which contribute to their genomic diversity. Despite their widespread presence in aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems, many aspects of their biology remain unknown, including the roles of lineage-specific ORFan genes (open reading frames with no detectable homologs in current databases) and the molecular strategies used to manipulate hosts. This Primer provides an accessible overview of protist-infecting giant viruses, summarizing their classification, virion architecture, replication strategies, and evolutionary scenarios, and points to key questions that remain open.

Journal of Virology.title: Primer: Human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1).
