Transcriptomic analysis identified 61 strain-specific differentially expressed genes between GX-C4- and GX-C5-infected groups, which were enriched in pathways related to muscle cytoskeleton regulation and motor protein function. The myosin gene MYH4 was significantly downregulated in GX-C4-infected cells, and the expression of the key immune molecule TICAM2 was also suppressed. The differential expression of these genes in host cells may further contribute to the differences in viral pathogenicity. Collectively, RSSL deletion significantly enhances viral pathogenic characteristics and reduces drug susceptibility, likely by promoting cytoskeletal rearrangement, and enhancing membrane fusion. These findings provide important theoretical insights into the differential pathogenicity of HIV-1 CRF01_AE Clusters 4 and 5.IMPORTANCEThis study identifies the RSSL tetrapeptide deletion in the gp41 region as a key molecular signature of CRF01_AE Cluster 4 strains and demonstrates its central role in enhancing viral replication capacity and resistance to fusion inhibitors through modulation of viral fusion efficiency. Notably, the RSSL-deleted strain exhibited up to 12-fold increased resistance to the clinical fusion inhibitor LP-98, suggesting that this deletion may impact therapeutic efficacy. Transcriptomic analysis further reveals enrichment in cytoskeletal pathways, the significant downregulation of MYH4 offering potential new targets for antiviral intervention. These findings provide a critical scientific basis for understanding the molecular evolution of CRF01_AE clusters, informing epidemic surveillance, and optimizing treatment strategies.

Journal of Virology.title: Natural variation in BtSARSr-CoV nsp12 harbors adaptive mutations that enhance viral replication and spillover risk in humans.
Journal of Virology.abstract: [UNLABELLED] The non-structural protein 12 (nsp12) is essential for SARS-related coronavirus (SARSr-CoV) replication and a major antiviral target, yet the functional significance of its natural variation in bat reservoirs remains unclear. Here, by analyzing 183 bat SARS-related coronavirus nsp12 sequences, we identified mutation hotspots that overlapped with sites variable in human SARS-CoV-2 variants (14 of 33 sites analyzed, including P323L), suggesting shared functional constraints across species. Using a cell-based reporter assay for high-throughput profiling of nsp12 function, we found that 8 of 21 bat-derived mutations enhanced polymerase activity at 37°C, with several also conferring an advantage at 33°C or 40°C. Four of these mutations (I171V, A185S, R249K, and N611S) increased replication in a SARS-CoV-2 replicon system, and all have emerged independently in circulating lineages (A185S reached detectable global prevalence by 2025). These mutations did not affect remdesivir sensitivity. Structurally, the mutations localize to regions involved in RNA capping or the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) catalytic core. Notably, SARS-CoV-related strains naturally encode multiple such adaptive residues, whereas SARS-CoV-2-related viruses retain ancestral states. Our study demonstrates that bat SARSr-CoV nsp12 variation pre-encodes mutations capable of enhancing human-cell replication, providing a predictive framework for monitoring polymerase changes with zoonotic potential. [IMPORTANCE] Bat SARS-related coronaviruses (BtSARSr-CoVs) are closely linked to past human pandemics and represent an ongoing source of zoonotic risk. Proactive evaluation of their spillover potential is therefore critical for pandemic preparedness. Current risk assessments have focused largely on receptor compatibility, with limited experimental investigation of viral replication fitness in human cells. In this study, we demonstrate that specific mutations in the viral RNA polymerase non-structural protein 12 (nsp12), naturally circulating in BtSARSr-CoVs, can enhance viral replication in both bat and human cells. By functionally validating several such mutations that later emerged in SARS-CoV-2, we establish a direct link between reservoir virus diversity and pathways of human adaptation. The high-throughput reporter platform developed here provides a scalable tool for prospectively assessing the replication fitness of nsp12 variants identified through surveillance. Together, these findings enhance our ability to interpret genetic signatures from animal coronaviruses and contribute to a more predictive framework for monitoring variants with zoonotic potential.

Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.title: Fragmented decision-making hinders the transition to sustainable sand alternatives
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment.abstract: Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00858-zSand extraction sustains development but destabilizes ecosystems. Transitioning to sustainable alternatives will require decision-making that reconciles sand’s economic, social and environmental values.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: TopoPPI: A geometry-aware platform for visualization and low-distortion mapping of protein-protein interaction interfaces
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Shuyu Zhong Protein–protein interfaces encode molecular recognition through spatially organized contacts, yet their buried, curved surfaces are difficult to inspect as a whole. Flattening these surfaces can expose interface organization but introduces geometric distortion and may divide individual residues into disconnected regions. We present TopoPPI, a geometry-aware platform that converts interaction surfaces into low-distortion two-dimensional atlases while retaining links to source atoms, residues and contacts. TopoPPI extends OptCuts with a contact-weighted penalty for seam-induced fragmentation of residue footprints—the surface regions assigned to individual residues—jointly balancing continuity, seam length and distortion. In a leakage-controlled benchmark of 2,236 experimental complexes, the geometry-only OptCuts foundation achieved 88.39% lower family-weighted scale-fair distortion than the next-best tested parameterization across 2,209 complete comparable outputs. Across 2,204 exact-domain comparisons, TopoPPI reduced family-weighted residue-footprint fragmentation by 12.81% (95% confidence interval, 11.50–14.05%), with a 2.60% increase in normalized seam length and a 0.061% increase in scale-fair distortion. Continuity gains extended to 1,180 fixed-pose pairs of AlphaFold monomer models and 145 predicted complexes, with fragmentation reductions of 18.60% and 11.65%, respectively. Functionally annotated antibody and colicin–immunity interfaces demonstrated reconnection of the footprints of experimentally characterized binding and specificity residues. Further applications mapped published binding and folding free-energy estimates onto the KRAS–RAF1 interface and compared shared receptor residues across two growth-hormone recognition sites. Available through graphical and command-line interfaces, TopoPPI provides a residue-aware visualization framework for integrating structural contacts and functional annotations within geometrically controlled interface maps.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: GapCNV: A comprehensive framework for CNV detection in low-input DNA sequencing data
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Xuanxuan Yu, Fei Qin, Shiwei Liu, Noah J. Brown, Xiao Fan, Qing Lu, Guoshuai Cai, Jennifer L. Guler, Feifei Xiao Copy number variants (CNVs) are prevalent in both diploid and haploid genomes and contribute to genome evolution and phenotypic diversity. However, CNV detection in low-input data, including low-cell and single-cell sequencing data, remains challenging due to the shallow and highly uneven read counts and amplification bias. Another challenge lies in selecting reference samples, which are used to provide a baseline for defining copy-number losses or gains. Normalization using references containing common CNVs can lead to cancellation of true CNV signals or false CNV calls. Here, we develop GapCNV, a statistical framework for CNV detection in low-input DNA sequencing data from both haploid and diploid genomes. GapCNV uses preliminary cell clustering and shared CNV profiles to construct bin-specific pseudo-references from cells inferred to have the copy-neutral state. This strategy reduces the incorporation of common CNVs into the normalization baseline and thereby preserves common CNV signals. We evaluated GapCNV using simulations with and without amplification biases and datasets from Plasmodium falciparum, human breast cancer and melanoma. In simulations, GapCNV achieved high precision rate while maintaining competitive sensitivity, with advantages for detecting short and common CNVs. In P. falciparum, GapCNV detected the known CNVs and recovered the short CNV more frequently than the benchmarking methods. In the melanoma cell line and human breast tumors, GapCNV recovered bulk or single-cell derived copy number profile across individual cells. These results show that adaptive, bin-specific pseudo-reference construction can improve CNV detection when reliable normal controls are unavailable.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Hierarchical data-driven dynamical surrogate models of social decision-making
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Manuel Brenner, Ismail Guennouni, Daniel Durstewitz, Stephanie N. L. Schmidt, Stefanie Lis, Peter Kirsch, Georgia Koppe Social decision making is inherently complex, shaped by dynamic trust building, biases, and adaptive strategies. Yet in laboratory settings, its study is often constrained by small datasets that nonetheless encode rich and sophisticated cognitive processes. This scarcity has historically limited modeling approaches to hand-tailored frameworks that embed strong priors about the underlying mechanisms. Recent advances in data-driven modeling of latent dynamical processes provide an alternative, extracting generative models directly from behavioral data without restrictive assumptions. Building on these methods, we derive hierarchical digital surrogates from sparse, non-Gaussian investment sequences in repeated trust games. Our approach proceeds in three stages. First, we demonstrate that, despite the limited data, the inferred models can accurately predict future investments and outperform theory-driven reinforcement-learning and Bayesian cognitive models, establishing predictive validity and providing a solid baseline for subsequent mechanistic analyses. Second, we analyze the latent dynamics of these models and show that they capture mechanistic structure in how investments and choice uncertainty are organized in state space and how social versus non-social cues are represented, in a way that parallels patterns observed directly in the empirical behavior. Third, we exploit the generative nature of the hierarchical digital surrogates to run in-silico experiments beyond the original data, such as probing how specific cues steer participants into trusting or mistrusting states and simulating responses to novel, unobserved cue-outcome combinations and trustee strategies. Together, this work demonstrates how generative digital surrogates open a new path toward mechanistic, data-driven accounts of social interaction dynamics that both reproduce observed behavior and support hypothesis generation in virtual environments.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: A beam–membrane biomechanical vocal fold model incorporating posturing and glottal conformation
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Mohamed A. Serry, Matías Zañartu, Sean D. Peterson The posture of the vocal folds produced by laryngeal muscle activation plays a central role in determining the dynamics of voice production. Abnormal vocal fold configurations are frequently associated with inefficient phonation and a variety of voice disorders. Although diverse glottal closure patterns have been observed clinically, the biomechanical mechanisms governing their dynamic behavior and resulting phonatory characteristics remain incompletely understood. Moreover, existing numerical models that incorporate the effects of the intrinsic musculature on posturing and glottal conformation are computationally expensive, which limits their suitability for large-scale parametric investigations. In this work, we introduce a computationally inexpensive vocal fold (VF) model wherein the body and cover VF layers are treated as a composite beam and a coupled membrane, respectively. Intrinsic laryngeal muscle activation, in addition to positioning the arytenoid cartilages and cricothyroid joint, introduces moments at the boundaries of the structure that influence glottal conformation. The model produces phonatory characteristics that are qualitatively consistent with those reported in high-fidelity finite-element models and clinical studies, thereby supporting its predictive capability while offering substantial computational advantage. The proposed framework provides biomechanical insights into the influence of incomplete glottal closure on phonation dynamics and may serve as a computationally tractable tool for investigating mechanisms underlying certain voice disorders.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Exploring the potential of bile fluid dynamics analysis to inform clinical strategies for choledochal cysts: Experimental and numerical studies
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Yidan Shang, Jiaying Liu, Wentao Sun, Renquan Tu, Xueren Li, Xiaojian Ni, Houbao Liu, Jiyuan Tu Surgical intervention is essential for choledochal cysts (CCs) due to their high lifetime risk of progressing to cholangiocarcinoma, yet management strategies vary worldwide. Given bile fluid’s vital role in digestion, investigating bile flow dynamics may provide surgeons with additional insights for treatment planning. In this study, one MRI-based healthy adult scan was used to reconstruct biliary system, which was then modified according to Todani classifications to generate eight CC types. Particle Image Velocimetry was used to first visualize local velocity field, followed by computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of bile emptying to analyze pathological non-Newtonian bile flow. Wall shear stress (WSS), a key biomechanical parameter, was visualized through 2D surface mapping for comparative evaluation. Results showed consistently low velocity in dilated regions, suggesting bile accumulation in CCs, particularly in Types 1a, 2, 4a, and 4b. While WSS changes were minimal in the healthy biliary system, extreme gradients, up to 10,000-fold emerged in CCs, especially Types 1a, 2, and 4a. These findings highlight that bile flow characteristics are primarily dictated by localized anatomical abnormalities, aligning with surgical interventions that target dilated regions. These findings demonstrate the potential of CFD to provide additional biomechanical insights into bile flow abnormalities associated with different CC types, which may serve as a reference for future clinical investigations.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Ontology pre-training improves machine learning-based predictions for metabolites
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Charlotte Tumescheit, Martin Glauer, Simon Flügel, Martin Larralde, Fabian Neuhaus, Till Mossakowski, Janna Hastings Deep learning has recently led to multiple breakthroughs in longstanding biological problems. Recent advances have shown that integration of expert knowledge can improve deep learning model predictive performance in complex domains such as biology. Bio-ontologies offer a rich source of curated biological knowledge that can be harnessed to this end. Here, we describe an intuitive and generalisable approach to embed the knowledge contained in a classification hierarchy derived from a bio-ontology into a deep learning model as an intermediate training step between general-purpose pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning: a process that we call’ontology pre-training’. We show that this approach leads to an improvement in predictive performance and a reduction in training time for a broad range of prediction tasks related to metabolite functions, activities and properties in living systems, using a range of datasets derived from MoleculeNet. We see the biggest improvement for regression tasks, e.g., prediction of lipophilicity and aqueous solubility of molecules, and a robust improvement for most classification tasks. Our approach can be adapted for a wide range of knowledge sources, models and prediction tasks.

PLOS Computational Biology.title: Exploring the mechanism of oxfendazole in inhibiting osteosarcoma-induced osteolysis based on single-cell RNA seqsuencing
PLOS Computational Biology.abstract: by Jifeng Miao, Pintian Wang, Wenyu Feng, Haiyi Quan, Yunhua Lin, Gejin Wei, Fake Meng, Shanhang Li, Mingxiu Yang, Binyuan Ning, Jingxin Deng, Liang Xiong, Jianming Hu, Yun Liu, Qingjun Wei Osteosarcoma-associated osteolysis represents a major obstacle in the management of osteosarcoma. Within the osteolytic microenvironment, interactions between osteoclasts and tumor cells facilitate tumor proliferation and metastatic dissemination, and contribute to the development of pathological fractures. However, conventional osteoclast-targeting agents are insufficient to effectively suppress osteosarcoma-driven bone resorption. In this study, single-cell RNA sequencing was performed to identify critical regulators involved in osteoclast differentiation in the context of osteosarcoma. Using the Beyondcell platform, drugs targeting osteoclast-related signaling pathways were screened, and oxfendazole (OFN) was identified as a potential therapeutic candidate, with ANXA2 recognized as a key associated target. In vitro osteoclastogenesis assays and an in vivo tibial orthotopic osteosarcoma model demonstrated that oral administration of OFN via gavage effectively suppressed osteoclast formation and osteolytic activity, as confirmed by micro-CT and histopathological analyses. But OFN alone did not significantly inhibit osteosarcoma growth but effectively reduced osteoclast-mediated osteolysis. In addition, qRT-PCR and immunohistochemistry confirmed that OFN downregulates ANXA2 expression in vitro and in vivo, thereby impairing osteoclast differentiation. Molecular dynamics simulations combined with in-vitro validation further suggested that OFN may interact with the transcription factor ZNF530, leading to reduced ANXA2 transcription. In conclusion, the integration of single-cell RNA sequencing with the Beyondcell algorithm enabled the identification of OFN as a potent candidate agent for osteosarcoma-induced osteolysis. OFN attenuates osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption by suppressing ANXA2 expression. These findings provide preclinical evidence supporting the therapeutic potential of OFN in the treatment of osteosarcoma-associated osteolysis.

mBio.title: Kappa prophage impacts Vibrio cholerae fitness and is restricted by the BREX phage defense system.
mBio.abstract: Vibrio cholerae's pathogenicity largely stems from the acquisition of cholera toxin genes via lysogenic conversion mediated by the CTX prophage. However, the strong association of other prophages with epidemic strains has not been linked to lysogenic conversion. During the first wave of the seventh cholera pandemic, the Kappa prophage was commonly found in clinical isolates and was later shown to confer a competitive fitness advantage in the environment and to accelerate evolution by stimulating horizontal gene transfer; however, its role in virulence remains unknown. Here, we report that the Kappa prophage confers a competitive fitness advantage in vitro and during intestinal tract infection in both Wave 1 and Wave 3 strains. This competitive fitness advantage is due to phage predation on neighboring cells, and not to lysogenic conversion. Furthermore, we show that loss of Kappa coincides with the acquisition of novel phage defense systems from SXT integrative and conjugative elements VchBan9 and VchInd5. Phage defense systems BREX and AbiC inhibited Kappa predation and restricted horizontal gene transfer, thereby reducing Kappa's competitive fitness advantage.IMPORTANCEAs prophages are found in many bacterial genomes, understanding their roles in bacterial fitness advances our understanding of bacterial evolution and virulence drivers. The work presented here contributes to our understanding of the temperate phage-host arms race and highlights how the acquisition of phage defense systems can be a double-edged sword in Vibrio cholerae, protecting it from phage predation, yet limiting lysogenic conversion and evolution.

mBio.title: Characterization of a novel plasmid-borne multigene cluster conferring high As and Sb resistance in Klebsiella pasteurii Sb-24.
mBio.abstract: Arsenic resistance operons are generally controlled by ArsR repressors, yet some ars loci encode extracytoplasmic function sigma factors whose roles remain unknown. We identified a plasmid-borne, bidirectional ars locus in Klebsiella pasteurii Sb-24, an isolate from antimony-contaminated soil with high resistance to arsenite and antimonite. The locus contains a canonical arsR1D1A1B1C1 module and a second module comprising arsN, arsA2, arsD2, sigZars, arsH, and arsR2. Exposure to arsenic and antimony compounds induced sigZars and multiple genes within the second module. Deletion of sigZars strongly reduced induction of arsN, arsA2, and arsD2, particularly during methylarsenite exposure, while having comparatively little effect on arsA1 and arsD1. The mutant also displayed reduced growth under selected inorganic and organic arsenical conditions and was outcompeted by the wild type during serial passage at low arsenite concentrations. These findings suggest that SigZars is required for full induction of a secondary ars module and support a multilayered regulatory architecture that broadens bacterial resistance to distinct arsenic species.IMPORTANCEArsenic and antimony contamination creates strong selection for resistance genes, many of which occur on mobile plasmids. In Klebsiella pasteurii Sb-24, a plasmid-borne resistance region contains a specialized sigma factor that is required for strong expression of a second detoxification module, particularly during exposure to organic arsenic compounds. Loss of this regulator reduced stress tolerance and competitive fitness at low arsenite concentrations. These results show that metalloid resistance can be controlled by layered regulatory systems rather than by a single metal-sensing repressor. The work broadens our understanding of how environmental bacteria adapt to mixed metalloid pollution and identifies a potentially mobile regulatory module relevant to arsenic cycling and environmental surveillance.

FEMS Microbiology Reviews.title: Phage-Host Dynamics in Food Systems: Rethinking the "Lytic" and "Temperate" Paradigm.
FEMS Microbiology Reviews.abstract: Phage-host dynamics are central to food systems because bacteriophages can threaten microbial stability while serving as tools for microbial control. In fermentations, phages compromise starter culture performance and product consistency, whereas in foods, animal production, and processing environments they are increasingly used as biocontrol agents against foodborne pathogens. Temperate phages may also influence virulence, tolerance, competition, and horizontal gene transfer, including antimicrobial resistance gene mobilization, placing phage ecology within a One Health framework. These roles have traditionally been interpreted through a binary model in which virulent phages lyse and temperate phages persist. However, reports of pseudolysogeny, carrier state, and delayed lysis have long suggested that this distinction is incomplete. Recent large-scale studies showing that virulent phages can persist through colony purification and bacterial genome assembly workflows provide the central motivation for this review. These findings suggest that long-term non-lysogenic association may be more widespread than appreciated and challenge the assumption that "lytic" phages necessarily cause immediate host elimination. In food systems, this has implications for fermentation reliability, biocontrol, surveillance, and One Health interpretation. We argue that food systems are informative settings for reassessing phage lifestyle categories, and that "lytic" should be understood as infection potential rather than guaranteed ecological outcome.

FEMS Microbiology Reviews.title: Engineering antimicrobial peptides through the design-build-test-learn framework.
FEMS Microbiology Reviews.abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has intensified the need for alternative anti-infective strategies. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer diverse mechanisms of action, but their translation remains constrained by poor physiological stability, host toxicity, and manufacturing costs. This review examines AMP development within a design-build-test-learn (DBTL) framework that connects computational discovery, peptide production, experimental evaluation, and iterative optimization. Proteome mining and generative artificial intelligence expand the accessible sequence space, while solid-phase synthesis, engineered microbial hosts, and cell-free systems convert selected sequences into testable molecules. Chemical modification and formulation provide complementary routes to improve stability and delivery. Standardized screening and in vivo studies then establish the evidence needed to prioritize candidates and inform subsequent design and production decisions. Throughout this cycle, activity must be optimized together with toxicity, stability, manufacturability, and delivery rather than treated as the sole measure of success. This review discusses applications in medicine, agriculture, food preservation, and biotechnology, and identifies remaining limitations in data quality, assay comparability, scale-up, and translational support. The DBTL framework provides a basis for coordinating these activities, although its practical value depends on experimentally validated feedback and application-specific development criteria.

Journal of Evolutionary Biology.title: Phenotypic conflicts within organisms.
Journal of Evolutionary Biology.abstract: Every trait in an organism reflects the formation of a particular phenotypic state jointly shaped by genotype, environment, and the intrinsic dynamics of a developing system. Traits, however, do not exist in isolation but are highly integrated, such that the formation of one phenotypic state can influence others, either across traits or among alternative states of the same trait. These interactions can create internal phenotypic conflicts when the formation of one state constrains or discourages the formation of another state. Here, we present a general framework to study such conflicts. The set of possible phenotypic states for any trait within an organism is embedded in a multidimensional space defined by genetic, dynamic epigenetic and environmental axes. Phenotypic conflicts emerge from interactions within and between such spaces, captured by phenotypic links that describe how a phenotypic state in one trait influences the axes' coordinates of the phenotypic spaces of other traits. We propose a conceptual description of how phenotypic conflicts arise during development, how they can shape evolutionary trajectories and how they may be managed during evolution. We present diverse examples spanning multiple levels of biological organization, suggesting that phenotypic conflicts are not rare exceptions but pervasive features of complex living systems. By explicitly conceptualizing the processes and mechanisms that connect phenotypic states, this framework can open new avenues for interdisciplinary research on the internal architecture of phenotype spaces and their importance for evolvability.

Microbiological Research.title: Bacterial extracellular vesicles in metabolic diseases: From pathogenic mediators to therapeutic carriers.
Microbiological Research.abstract: The incidence of metabolic diseases (e.g. obesity, diabetes, and osteoporosis) is rising year by year worldwide. The gut microbiota, as a complex microbial ecosystem, is closely associated with the onset and progression of various metabolic diseases due to its dysbiosis. Recent studies have shown that extracellular vesicles derived from gut microbiota play a crucial role in bacterial-host communication. However, the specific roles and mechanisms of bacterial extracellular vesicles (bEVs) in metabolic diseases remain to be further explored. This review summarizes the biogenesis and composition of bEVs and critically examines their dual roles in the pathogenesis and treatment of metabolic diseases. We further discuss recent research progress on engineering strategies, including parental strain engineering, cargo loading, and surface functionalization to optimize the therapeutic efficacy of bEVs. Finally, we highlight key translational challenges and future prospects in bEVs-based development. This review aims to provide a theoretical foundation and new intervention strategies for the treatment of metabolic diseases.

Microbiological Research.title: A Streptomyces-derived cyclic peptide valinomycin primes two-layered plant local immunity and systemic disease resistance.
Microbiological Research.abstract: Intensive research has led to the identification of various natural compounds as alternative and complementary agents for the chemical management of plant diseases. Here, we propose that valinomycin, a cyclic peptide produced by Streptomyces bacillaris S8, is a putative biocontrol agent against various plant pathogens with dual functions. The compound demonstrated antifungal activity against the plant pathogenic fungus, Botrytis cinerea (B. cinerea), a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that causes gray mold disease in many plant species. Intriguingly, valinomycin boosted plant immunity with priming activity in response to pathogen infection. Plants treated with valinomycin exhibited an increased flg22-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation, and callose deposition, known hallmarks of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)-triggered immunity (PTI). Regarding effector-triggered immunity (ETI), valinomycin potentiated hypersensitive response (HR), a representative phenotype of the ETI responses. Furthermore, ROS burst assay revealed that valinomycin simultaneously facilitated PTI and ETI that mutually strengthen each other. Valinomycin increased the resistance against Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 (Pto DC3000), without antibacterial activity. Valinomycin primes plant immunity by modulating plant hormone crosstalk, extending to systemic resistance in Arabidopsis. Notably, valinomycin also enhanced disease resistance in tobacco and soybean, demonstrating its potential for expanded application to many crop species. Therefore, our study highlights valinomycin as a versatile natural compound with potential as a biocontrol agent, combining direct antifungal activity with plant immune-priming function across multiple plant species.

Water Research.title: Induction-heated interfacial catalysis for self-cleaning membrane distillation for complex brines.
Water Research.abstract: Membrane distillation (MD) can desalinate complex hypersaline brines, but practical operation is limited by temperature polarization and interfacial fouling or wetting. Here we introduce induction heating catalytic membrane distillation (IH-CMD), a reaction-separation platform that couples non-contact electromagnetic heating with peroxymonosulfate (PMS) activation at a PTFE-CoCu@Fe3O4 membrane-water interface. Under an alternating electromagnetic field, the PTFE-CoCu@Fe3O4 membrane achieved rapid interfacial heating (e.g., up to 210°C within one minute in air), which effectively mitigates temperature polarization and enhancing vapor flux by more than 3-fold compared to conventional MD. The hydroxyl-rich CoCu layer provided PMS-active sites and supported a hydrated outer interface; spectroscopy revealed induction-associated changes in surface hydroxylation, while density functional theory showed that hydroxylation state regulated PMS adsorption and polarization. This thermally regulated interface promoted catalytic oxidation, proposed to involve singlet oxygen and radical pathways alongside Co/Cu redox cycling, while improving resistance under gypsum-, surfactant-, oil-, and PFAS-containing conditions. Hollow-fiber membrane tests further demonstrated compatibility with a solenoid-coupled module and achieved 33.48 kg·m-2·h-1 freshwater production. These results establish an interface-centered heat-reaction-mass-transfer strategy for self-cleaning MD of complex hypersaline brines.

Water Research.title: Root mucilage-inspired hydrogel composite membranes enable high-efficacy ammonia recovery.
Water Research.abstract: Ammonia recovery from wastewater via membrane stripping is a compelling route for pollution control and nutrient recycling, yet its deployment is hindered by a trade-off between permeation flux and fouling resistance. Inspired by plant root mucilage, which enriches and transports nutrients from soil to roots, we present a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane coated with a mucilage-like hydrogel layer for ammonia (NH3) recovery. This biomimetic coating, fabricated from chitosan (CS) and sodium alginate (SA), mimics functional traits of root mucilage. Abundant polar groups in the hydrogel layer promote NH3 partitioning and localized NH3 enrichment, thereby improving interfacial NH3 supply, while the highly hydrated network facilitates NH3 diffusion at a rate comparable to that in bulk solution. Together, these features offset the transport penalty imposed by the dense hydrogel layer. Concurrently, this coating enhances antifouling performance through a smoother surface, sub-nanometre size sieving, hydration shielding, and Donnan exclusion. In a 180-h real-digestate test, the PVDF@CS/SA membrane maintained an NH3 flux comparable to that of the pristine PVDF membrane, yet showed a lower fouling-induced flux decline (7% vs. 56%). This work provides a new paradigm for developing advanced antifouling membranes that overcome the permeation flux-fouling resistance trade-off.

Water Research.title: Anodic boundary-layer pumping enables membraneless organophosphonate conversion and phosphorus recovery in recirculating cooling water.
Water Research.abstract: Organophosphonate antiscalants in recirculating cooling water resist degradation and limit phosphorus (P) recovery. Here, an anodic-pumping-enhanced membraneless electrochemical system (A-MFES) was developed to couple organophosphonate conversion with P recovery. Directional pumping through a porous Ti/PbO2 anode enhanced contact with electroactive surfaces and transported the acidic interfacial solution containing reactive chlorine into the pumped effluent. Pumping controls, free-chlorine measurements, and quenching responses supported the coupling of interfacial oxidation with continued chlorine-mediated solution-phase oxidation, extending oxidant utilization beyond the electrode surface. Using ethylenebis(nitrilodimethylene) tetraphosphonic acid (EDTMP) as the representative compound, A-MFES achieved 57.1% oxidation during single-pass operation and also converted structurally distinct organophosphonate antiscalants. Coupling with a pumped-cathode precipitation unit enabled 59.6% P recovery as hydroxyapatite-containing calcium phosphate, with 63.5% oxidation in the coupled process. Sustained oxidation during continuous operation and conversion in real recirculating cooling water supported the applicability of the oxidation unit. In high-hardness synthetic cooling water, the integrated process achieved 60.0% EDTMP oxidation and 49.5% P recovery alongside sequential hardness removal. This study establishes directional anodic pumping as a strategy for extending interfacial oxidation into the effluent and integrating organophosphonate conversion with mineral recovery in a membraneless process.

Water Research.title: Meta-omics deciphers the role of migratory bird feces-derived phages in promoting the persistence of ARGs in opportunistic pathogens in the Yangtze Estuary wetlands.
Water Research.abstract: Migratory birds are well-documented antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) transboundary vectors, yet fecal ARG persistence in estuarine wetlands remains poorly understood. To explain this issue, we profiled metagenomic/viromic data across pre-arrival, staging, departure phases in the Yangtze Estuary, a world-class conservation wetland. Migratory bird feces had significantly lower ARG loads than local free-range duck feces as contrast (T-test, P < 0.01, n = 32), but harbored distinct resistance profiles dominated bacA (bacitracin), bla1 (β-lactam), and arnA (peptide) resistance genes. Bird arrivals triggered waterborne ARG surges to -0.88 ± 0.16 log10 (ARGs/cell) (P < 0.01, n = 30), while sedimentary resistomes stayed stable (One-way ANOVA test, P > 0.05, n = 24). Pronounced taxonomic differences between avian and wetland bacteria restricted most ARG-carrying bacteria to short-term existence. However, some opportunistic pathogens (e.g. Escherichia, Pseudomonas) achieved stable niches via deterministic niche selection, serving as shared host genera for avian and environmental phages. Unlike the bulk metagenomic ARGs correlating strongly with bacterial community structure (Spearman, Rho = 0.43, P < 0.01), viromic ARGs were decoupled from phage dynamics and minimally responsive to physicochemical stressors (Mantel test, R2 = 0.11 vs. 0.32, P < 0.01). MetaCHIP analysis of Nanopore-Illumina hybrid assembled bins from viable communities detected 3 transferred contigs associated with plasmids. Meanwhile, phage-associated ARGs derived from wild birds exploited opportunistic pathogens as hosts to sustain persistence in wetlands. These findings reveal that conventional bacteria-centric monitoring underestimates avian-borne antimicrobial resistance in the Yangtze Estuary wetland, calling for virome-inclusive management there.

Water Research.title: Which uncertainties matter? Global sensitivity analysis of model-based and data-driven leakage detection methods via sparse-grid stochastic collocation.
Water Research.abstract: Leakages in water distribution networks cause water loss globally, jeopardize water quality, and increase energy consumption for water supply. While numerous software-based detection methods to enable prompt leakage detection have been proposed in the literature, most are developed using synthetic data that fails to represent the range of errors and operating conditions encountered in practice. To address this gap, we conduct a variance-based global sensitivity analysis of the detection performance of two state-of-the-art leakage detection methods, data-driven and model-based, under uncertainties in the number of pressure sensors, sensor accuracy, hydraulic model parameters, and a method hyperparameter. To keep the analysis tractable, we use sparse-grid stochastic collocation, reducing the number of model evaluations by orders of magnitude relative to Monte Carlo. We assess convergence, robustness, and credibility of the estimates. In this study, sensor number and measurement accuracy dominate detection performance for both methods, whereas hydraulic parameters and the detection threshold are secondary; finer rankings among the remaining inputs differ by leakage type and method but often fall within the estimated uncertainty. The two methods fail in different regimes, motivating hybrid strategies that combine their strengths.

Water Research.title: Chlorination of a chlorothalonil metabolite (R471811) and aniline: Kinetics and mechanisms.
Water Research.abstract: Chlorothalonil metabolites (CMs) have been detected ubiquitously and persistently in European groundwater, despite the ban of chlorothalonil in the European Union and Switzerland in 2019. Among the six frequently detected CMs, CM (R471811), which contains two amide groups and one sulfonic acid moiety, has been detected most frequently and at the highest concentrations. This metabolite has been shown to be partially abated during mild chlorination, despite its limited removal by ozonation or hydroxyl radical-driven advanced oxidation processes, thereby warranting further investigation of its chlorination kinetics and mechanisms. CM was found to react primarily with hypochlorite via nucleophilic attack at the two amide nitrogen atoms, exhibiting distinct species-specific second-order rate constants of 24 M-1s-1 and 0.19 M-1s-1, respectively for the two reaction steps. The reaction initially yielded N-chloramides, which subsequently underwent a Hofmann rearrangement to form an aniline-type compound. The rearrangement from aromatic N-chloramide to aniline was confirmed during chlorination of the model compound 2,4,5-trichlorobenzamide with the detection of 2,4,5-trichloroaniline. To elucidate the fate of aniline, its kinetics and mechanisms for the reaction with chlorine were further investigated. Chlorination of aniline was dominated by hypochlorous acid, with an apparent second-order rate constant of 4.9 × 104 M-1s-1 at pH 7. The reaction is proposed to initially form N-chloroaniline, followed by cleavage of the NCl bond generating phenylnitrenium cations, leaving the ortho and para positions available for nucleophilic substitution. As a consequence, 2-chloroaniline, 4-chloroaniline, and 4-aminophenol were detected as initial chlorination products. Subsequently, 2-chloroaniline was transformed to 4-amino-3-chlorophenol, while a fraction of 4-aminophenol was further oxidized to the potentially toxic products, 4-nitroso- and 4-nitrophenol, with yields of ≤ 4.5%.

Briefings in Bioinformatics.title: CausalMut: a causal deep learning framework for enzyme mutational effect prediction
Briefings in Bioinformatics.abstract: AbstractAccurate prediction of enzyme mutational effects on catalytic kinetics is fundamental to data-driven enzyme engineering, yet existing deep learning models are fundamentally constrained by biases inherent in the data generation process. Experimental datasets are conditioned on prevailing experimental choices rather than uniform mutation interventions, which introduces spurious correlations that compromise model generalization. To address this challenge, CausalMut is proposed as a causality-guided deep learning framework that disentangles genuine mutational causal effects from confounding biases. The data generation mechanism is first formalized via a structural causal graph, revealing the experimental environment as a confounder that induces distributional imbalance across mutation types. Building on this analysis, CausalMut integrates two components: a Multi-scale Interaction Enhanced Network (MIENet), which captures complex interactions among the wild-type enzyme, substrate, and mutant without 3D structural information; and a Joint Focal-IPS optimization strategy, which corrects distributional imbalances at both the amino-acid and mutant levels. Comprehensive experiments on three real-world enzyme kinetic datasets ($k_{\text{cat}}$, $K_{m}$, and $k_{\text{cat}}/K_{m}$) against five state-of-the-art baselines demonstrate average improvements of 16.24% in root mean square error and 22.19% in $R^{2}$. CausalMut maintains consistent superiority under three biologically motivated distribution-shift settings, and case studies further demonstrate its ability to identify high-activity variants within a fixed screening budget, validating its robustness and practical utility.

Current Biology.title: A theory of generalized vector coding and subicular function
Current Biology.abstract: Wang and Bicanski propose a theory of subicular coding. Discontinuities in the world drive geometric representations in the subiculum, including boundary vector cells and corner cells. The framework generalizes to other domains, natural environments, and population responses, explaining seemingly different neural correlates as manifestations of the same principle.

They show that the actin-binding protein SCAB1 organizes F-actin around small vacuoles, facilitating their spatial proximity to the central vacuole and providing a mechanism linking cytoskeletal organization to vacuolar fusion.

Current Biology.title: Whole-genome phylogenomics and synteny support a single origin of body-plan asymmetry in flatfishes
authors: Julian Gallego-Garcia, Delson Hays, Pakorn Tongboonkua, Jeremiah J. Minich, Leon Hilgers, Todd P. Michael, Michael Hiller, Guillermo Ortí, Dahiana Arcila, Wayne Pfeiffer, Emanuell Duarte-Ribeiro, Siavash Mirarab, Ricardo Betancur-R.
Current Biology.abstract: Whether flatfish asymmetry evolved once or more than once has been debated for over a century. Gallego-Garcia et al. combine whole-genome phylogenomics with gene-order data from 17 fish genomes, including the first chromosome genome for Psettodes, and find that nucleotide and microsynteny evidence support a single origin of the flatfish body plan.

eLife.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication
eLife.abstract: The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

eLife.title: Adaptation of an herbivorous arthropod to green tea plants by overcoming catechin defenses
eLife.abstract: Green tea catechins protect tea plants from biotic stressors. Among herbivorous mites, the generalist Tetranychus urticae has not been reported as a tea pest. In contrast, some populations of Tetranychus kanzawai thrive on tea plants. Here, we investigated the mechanism of this adaptation. Green tea catechins were repellent and toxic to T. urticae and tea non-adapted T. kanzawai and had an antifeedant effect on the latter. We identified an intradiol ring-cleavage dioxygenase DOG15, a gene horizontally transferred from fungi, as required for the adaptation of T. kanzawai to tea plants. Tea feeding strongly induces DOG15 expression in tea-adapted T. kanzawai, with mRNA and protein levels up to 31.6 and 12.1 times higher than in tea-fed T. urticae. We also identified two amino acid substitutions in DOG15 between the two Tetranychus species that increased the catechin-cleaving activity of the T. kanzawai enzyme. These substitutions predispose T. kanzawai but not T. urticae for the adaptation to tea plants. Inducible expression of modified DOG15 then enables T. kanzawai to efficiently detoxify green tea catechins. Our findings reveal how a horizontally transferred gene can be co-opted through structural and regulatory changes to overcome plant chemical defenses.

eLife.title: Transposons contribute to splice-isoform diversity in the Drosophila brain
eLife.abstract: The extraordinary complexity of the brain depends in part on the vast diversity of mRNA isoforms it expresses, often in a cell-type specific manner. In a recent study, we found that intronic transposable elements (TEs) are spliced into neural transcripts and diversify the splice isoform repertoire of neurons and glia (Treiber and Waddell, 2020). A recent paper by Azad et al. revisits these findings using their TIDAL analysis pipeline applied to our published data (Azad et al., 2024). Their analysis did not find any of the splicing reads we reported and although they used RT-PCR to test seven of the 264 TE–gene pairs we had previously reported, they failed to validate TE–gene splicing in any of them. Here, we conduct a quantitative analysis of TE exonisation and show that intronic TE insertions are frequently recruited as alternative exons, with exon usage ranging from rare events to near-complete inclusion in transcripts. We implement this analysis in an improved version of our TEChim software and present clear support for TE–gene splicing at the seven loci tested by Azad et al. We also identify methodological issues in the experimental and computational design of the Azad et al. study that likely explains their failure to detect TE–gene chimeras, while demonstrating that TE–gene splicing can be detected by RT-PCR under appropriate experimental conditions. Together, our data demonstrates that TE splice isoforms are not rare artefacts but measurable and biologically relevant features of the Drosophila brain transcriptome that may contribute to the molecular complexity and functional adaptability of the brain.

Nature Reviews Genetics.title: Generative genome design with DNA language models
Nature Reviews Genetics.abstract: Nature Reviews Genetics, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41576-026-01032-3In this Tools of the Trade article, Samuel King illustrates how genome language models can generate complete bacteriophage genomes from learned DNA sequence patterns. He discusses the design, synthesis and validation of AI-generated phages, highlighting new opportunities for genome-scale biological engineering.

Nature Genetics.title: Integrated QTL mapping and CRISPR screening in pooled iPSC-derived microglia reveals genetic drivers of neurodegenerative risk
Nature Genetics.abstract: Nature Genetics, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02843-0This study presents a scalable framework for understanding the genetic determinants of gene expression and cellular phenotype in stem-cell-derived microglia-like cells and linking these to neurodegenerative disease.

Nature Genetics.title: Evolutionary lineage-specific and heterochromatin-independent repression of transposon-derived sequences
Nature Genetics.abstract: Nature Genetics, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02823-4This study identifies SCAN zinc-finger proteins as rapidly evolving transcription factors that target lineage-specific transposable elements and restrict their regulatory activity without canonical repressive chromatin modifications.

Cell Reports.title: Rescue from the bottom of the (beta) barrel: Outer mitochondrial membrane quality control
Cell Reports.abstract: β-barrel proteins are critical gatekeepers of the outer mitochondrial membrane, yet the mechanisms underpinning their quality control are largely unexplored. Here, Kämmerer et al. identify three AAA-ATPases that extract and facilitate the degradation of translocation-arrested β-barrel proteins.

Molecular Biology and Evolution.title: Not all inflammation is equal: biomarker-structural discordance and flare risk in clinically stable small-bowel Crohn’s disease
Molecular Biology and Evolution.abstract: AbstractBackgroundPatients with clinically stable small-bowel Crohn’s disease (SB-CD) may harbor heterogeneous residual inflammation. We performed the first study characterizing inflammatory burden with video capsule endoscopy (VCE), intestinal ultrasound (IUS), and biomarkers, comparing their prognostic performance.MethodsPooled analysis of 3 prospective cohorts of adults with SB-CD in remission/mild symptoms (Crohn’s disease activity index [CDAI] n = 87); outcome analyses included 81 patients with follow-up.ResultsAmong 87 patients (median age 31, 57% male), 3 clusters emerged: low-burden (n = 48), biomarker-predominant (n = 18; markedly elevated FCP/CRP, preserved bowel wall thickness [BWT], intermediate Lewis score [LS]), and concordant-active (n = 21; uniform elevation across modalities). Twenty flare events (25%) occurred at median 12.5 months. Concordant-active carried higher flare risk than low-burden (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 2.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-7.11), while biomarker-predominant showed no significant excess risk (HR 1.00). In the SB-restricted comparison, SB-BWT plus FCP showed discrimination comparable to LS (C-index 0.635 vs. 0.596), and LS did not add to this combination (likelihood ratio test P = .223). Whole-bowel BWT ≥ 4.3 mm added to LS (P = .008), whereas SB-BWT ≥3.8 mm did not (P = .384).ConclusionsIsolated biomarker elevation without structural activity was not associated with significant excess flare risk in clinically stable SB-CD, while concordant activity showed higher risk requiring larger-cohort confirmation. Within the SB, IUS plus FCP showed no significant difference in prognostic performance compared with VCE, with whole-bowel IUS additionally contributing colonic transmural information not captured by the LS.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Rapid detection of beta-lactamase genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli from positive blood cultures using nanopore sequencing.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli are major Enterobacterales pathogens that commonly harbor beta-lactamase enzymes conferring antimicrobial resistance. Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) is time-consuming and may delay appropriate antibiotic treatment, whereas nanopore sequencing enables real-time genetic analysis and may support rapid antimicrobial resistance detection at the point of care. This study evaluated the performance of nanopore sequencing for detecting ceftriaxone and carbapenem resistance in positive blood cultures containing K. pneumoniae or E. coli. In this cross-sectional descriptive study, positive blood culture samples yielding K. pneumoniae or E. coli were analyzed. Bacterial DNA was extracted and sequenced in its native form using the PromethION nanopore platform to detect antimicrobial resistance genes, and sequencing-based predictions were compared with routine blood culture results and standard AST. A total of 62 K. pneumoniae and 96 E. coli samples met the inclusion criteria for DNA extraction and sequencing. Simulated real-time analysis showed that the optimal condition for detecting third-generation cephalosporin and carbapenem resistance genes was approximately 1 h of sequencing, using a sequence divergence threshold of <0.001 against the antimicrobial resistance gene database. For third-generation cephalosporin resistance, sensitivity was 87.0% (95% CI: 79.5%-94.5%) and specificity was 77.8% (95% CI: 68.7%-86.8%); for carbapenem resistance, sensitivity was 77.8% (95% CI: 58.6%-97.0%) and specificity was 96.4% (95% CI: 93.4%-99.5%). Overall, nanopore sequencing is feasible for rapid detection of ceftriaxone and carbapenem resistance directly from positive blood cultures, although further optimization is needed to improve accuracy.IMPORTANCEBloodstream infections can progress rapidly and require timely selection of effective antimicrobial therapy. However, conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing typically requires 2-3 days, which may delay optimal treatment. In this study, nanopore sequencing detected key antimicrobial resistance genes in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae directly from positive blood cultures after approximately 1 h of sequencing. This approach could support earlier prediction of antibiotic resistance and help guide more timely treatment decisions for patients with serious infections. The study also identified important limitations, including incorrect predictions for ceftriaxone and carbapenem resistance in some samples. Overall, these findings highlight the potential of rapid DNA sequencing to improve the management of bloodstream infections, while emphasizing that further improvement in predictive accuracy is needed before routine implementation in clinical laboratories.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Characterization of six environmental coliphages isolated in Astana, Kazakhstan, during the School of Molecular and Theoretical Biology.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Bacteriophage (phage) collections are essential resources for studying virus-host interactions in bacterial species. Here, we report six Escherichia coli-infecting phages that expand the Lund Collection of Bacteriophages. These phages were isolated in 2025 within the framework of the School of Molecular and Theoretical Biology for high school students, from samples collected in Lake Small Taldykol, Astana, Kazakhstan, using E. coli strains MG1655 ΔRM and EV36 as hosts. The isolated phages comprise Taldykol (LuPh6), a member of the genus Kagunavirus; Aidakhar (LuPh7) of the genus Phapecoctavirus; Samruk (LuPh8) of the genus Tequintavirus; the T-odd-like phage Baiterek (LuPh9) of the genus Vequintavirus; and two T-even-like phages, Tulpar (LuPh10) and Shurale (LuPh11), that belong to the genus Tequatrovirus. This expanded phage collection enhances the toolkit for investigating phage-host interactions and their molecular mechanisms and highlights the use of phage isolation as a component of high school research education.IMPORTANCEPhage collections are a key resource for studying phage biology, phage-bacteria interactions, and bacterial immune systems. Here, we extend the Lund Phage Collection through the isolation and characterization of six Escherichia coli-infecting phages, including three novel species (LuPh6, LuPh8, and LuPh11), as well as a member of the genus Phapecoctavirus (LuPh7) that is not sufficiently represented in widely used collections such as BASEL. This study expands the resources available for probing phage-host interactions and demonstrates an example of integrating phage research into the education of high school students.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Biological activities of Rhodobacter sphaeroides-derived extracellular vesicles through growth condition optimization.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-enclosed nanoparticles that transport bioactive cargo and can modulate host cellular responses. Rhodobacter sphaeroides is a metabolically versatile bacterium whose physiology is strongly shaped by oxygen availability, yet how oxygen-dependent growth states influence EV production, cargo composition, and bioactivity has remained insufficiently defined. Here, EVs were isolated from R. sphaeroides cultured under aerobic or anaerobic conditions and systematically compared using nanoparticle tracking analysis, electron microscopy, cargo quantification, comparative proteomics, and functional assays in mammalian cell models. Anaerobic cultivation increased EVs particle yield relative to aerobic cultivation while maintaining a similar mean vesicle size in the ~120 nm range, with both preparations dominated by small vesicles. EVs' cargo profiles differed between conditions, with anaerobic EVs showing higher preparation-level protein content and a distinct proteomic profile compared with aerobic EVs. Functionally, both EV preparations reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS)-associated fluorescence and increased fibroblast wound confluence in scratch assays, with preparation-dependent differences observed in the wound healing response. In lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophage-like cells, EVs modulated inflammatory transcription in a marker-specific manner: aerobic EVs showed stronger decreases in IL-1β and IL-6, whereas anaerobic EVs generally maintained comparatively higher expression for these markers; inducible nitric oxide synthase transcripts remained near the LPS-only level. Together, these findings indicate that oxygen availability serves as a scalable, non-genetic handle to tune R. sphaeroides EVs yield, protein cargo profiles, and context-dependent bioactivity, supporting culture-state optimization as a strategy for application-oriented EVs production.IMPORTANCECulture parameters are a major, yet often underused, control point for bacterial extracellular vesicles (EVs) engineering and standardization. This study shows that oxygen availability reshapes Rhodobacter sphaeroides EVs yield and protein cargo profiles while preserving a comparable nanoscale size regime, and those oxygen-tuned EVs preparations exhibit distinct functional profiles in ROS-associated fluorescence, wound-repair support, and inflammatory gene regulation. The transcriptional data further highlight that EVs-mediated immunomodulation is marker specific rather than uniformly pro- or anti-inflammatory, emphasizing the need for fit-for-purpose bioassays alongside physicochemical characterization. These results provide a practical framework for producing application-oriented R. sphaeroides EVs using scalable, non-genetic culture-state optimization.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Yeast culture extract of grape seed meal attenuates ETEC K88-induced inflammation in host by modulating AHL-like quorum-sensing signaling molecules.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is a primary pathogen inducing diarrhea in young animals. ETEC colonization and proliferation rely on quorum sensing (QS), predominantly mediated by N-acyl homoserine lactone (AHL) signal molecules. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether yeast culture extracts relieve intestinal inflammation via interfering with ETEC QS systems. This study aimed to investigate whether grape seed meal-derived Saccharomyces cerevisiae culture (GSMSC) mitigates inflammatory responses in ETEC K88-challenged BALB/c mice through regulating AHL-type QS signaling. GSMSC substantially alleviated ETEC K88-triggered intestinal injury, inflammatory reaction, and intestinal barrier impairment in mice. Mechanistically, GSMSC suppressed intestinal inflammation and oxidative stress by modulating fecal butyric acid, AHL, and 3-oxo-C12-HSL concentrations, reshaping the relative abundance of Odoribacter, and regulating the production of methyl (9E)-9-hexadecenoate. Collectively, these correlational findings highlight AHL-like QS molecules as a potential biomarker and regulatory target associated with the colonization and growth of ETEC K88 in the host.IMPORTANCEEnterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) is a primary cause of diarrhea in young animals, and its intestinal colonization depends on N-acyl homoserine lactone (AHL)-mediated quorum sensing (QS). However, few effective natural agents targeting QS have been identified to alleviate ETEC-triggered intestinal inflammation. This study demonstrated that grape seed meal-derived Saccharomyces cerevisiae culture extracts (GSMSCs) mitigate intestinal injury, inflammatory response, and barrier dysfunction in ETEC K88-infected mice via modulating QS signals, gut microbiota, and microbial metabolites. These correlational findings suggest that AHL-type QS may represent a promising regulatory target to mitigate ETEC infection, and hint at a potential natural quorum-quenching strategy for alleviating pathogen-triggered intestinal inflammation.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Supporting public health outbreak investigations with improved Legionella pneumophila isolate recovery using a comprehensive culture algorithm including an off-label use of a Legionella detection kit.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Legionella pneumophila (Lpn) is a gram-negative, fastidious environmental pathogen that is the major cause of Legionnaires' disease (LD). In New York State (NYS), Lpn is responsible for multiple outbreaks each year. For source attribution during an outbreak, whole-genome sequencing of culture isolates is needed to assess relatedness. Isolation of Lpn from clinical and environmental samples may pose challenges due to overgrowth of competing organisms and the potential for the initiation of patient antimicrobial treatment prior to specimen collection. In this study, we evaluated the IDEXX Legiolert method to improve recovery of Lpn isolates in both PCR-positive clinical specimens and environmental water samples. Our initial prospective study of 43 respiratory (RES) and 16 environmental samples found that isolate recovery of Lpn was improved by 25.6% for RES specimens and 43.8% for non-potable (NP) water samples when IDEXX Legiolert method was compared to our existing culture method. When the validated IDEXX Legiolert method was employed during several major outbreaks in NYS over the course of 4 years (2019-2023), encompassing 22 RES and 68 environmental samples, Lpn recovery was also improved (35% RES, 42% NP), further confirming the significant impact the IDEXX Legiolert has on outbreak source attribution. [IMPORTANCE] Legionnaires' disease (LD) is a serious and potentially lethal form of pneumonia, primarily resulting from the inhalation of aerosols contaminated with Legionella from artificial water supply or cooling systems. LD is frequently underdiagnosed due to its lack of distinguishing clinical presentation, rarity as a cause of pneumonia, and need for specialized testing. Furthermore, obtaining a lower respiratory specimen from LD cases is often challenging, and even when these specimens are available, culturing requires specific media that may not be available in all microbiology laboratories. In the present study, we assessed and implemented a modification to the culture procedure that improved Legionella pneumophila isolate recovery from PCR-positive samples. This innovative method, utilizing an off-label IDEXX Legiolert culture step, provides an improvement over current methods for determining source attribution of LD outbreaks, particularly in situations where isolating Legionella is challenging.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Perinatal influences on the gut resistome and bacteriome in South African infants from birth to 6 months of life: insights from a shotgun metagenomics study.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Antibiotic resistance (AR) is a major global health threat, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where neonatal infections remain a leading cause of death, compounded by limited surveillance and uncontrolled antibiotic use. The neonatal gut is a reservoir for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), yet LMIC data remain scarce. Using shotgun metagenomics, we investigated gut resistome and bacteriome dynamics in infants during their first 6 months of life. Analysis of 68 longitudinal fecal samples from 17 infants revealed 211 ARGs across 7 antibiotic classes. Beta-lactam genes (blaTEM-1 and blaTEM-10-MGH-1) dominated, accounting for 64.0% of detections and indicating substantial early-life resistance load. Non-blaTEM ARGs (e.g., cat4, tetC, aphA2) emerged between 16 and 26 weeks, reflecting ongoing microbial evolution. In this small, exploratory cohort, infant antibiotic exposure, maternal HIV with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), and cesarean delivery with maternal antibiotics were associated with higher ARG diversity; given the small, uneven subgroups, this pattern is hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive, suggesting a role for clinical and maternal factors in resistome development. The bacteriome featured diverse, resilient taxa with persistent opportunistic pathogens, including Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus, which are potential ARG reservoirs. Despite sample size limitations, these findings offer valuable insight into neonatal ARG acquisition, persistence, and bacterial profiles in an LMIC setting, and point to a plausible, multifactorial interplay of maternal, clinical, and environmental influences on resistome dynamics requiring confirmation in larger cohorts. This early, pervasive resistance reservoir supports tailored antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and microbiome-informed strategies, alongside future genotypic-phenotypic surveillance.IMPORTANCEThis study provides region-specific insight into the early-life gut resistome and bacteriome of infants from a low- and middle-income setting, addressing a gap in global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance. Universal detection of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from birth highlights the establishment of a genetic resistance reservoir, even in antibiotic-naïve populations. In this small, exploratory cohort, perinatal factors, including antibiotic exposure, maternal HIV/HAART status, and delivery mode, showed patterns associated with resistome diversity and microbial succession. Although not statistically definitive, these findings suggest multifactorial drivers of early AMR emergence warranting confirmation in larger studies. Persistence of clinically important ARGs alongside opportunistic pathogens raises questions for neonatal infection management; however, these genotypic findings indicate potential rather than confirmed resistance, underscoring the need for paired phenotypic susceptibility data. This work establishes foundational longitudinal data for South Africa, informing antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention, and microbiome-informed interventions to mitigate AMR risk and improve infant health outcomes.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Phylogenetic evidence of genetic diversity in Metamycoplasma salivarium from Saudi ventilator-associated pneumonia.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Culture-based identification of Metamycoplasma salivarium in ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is prone to misinterpretation due to phenotypic similarity with pathogenic Mycoplasma species. We performed full-length 16S rRNA PacBio sequencing on 24 M. salivarium sequence variants from Saudi ICU patients with VAP. Global alignments against four GenBank reference strains and phylogenetic reconstruction using neighbor-joining methods characterized population structure relative to global M. salivarium diversity. Twenty-three sequences (S1-S8, S10-S24) exhibited 99.6%-99.8% similarity to NBRC 14478 (Japan), 98.2%-98.4% similarity to 59271 (USA), and 97.3%-97.5% similarity to PG20 (Sweden), forming five phylogenetic clusters tightly associated with M. struthionis (NR_178373.1). Sequence S9 consistently diverged (91.6%-93.3% similarity), while S6 showed alignment-specific variation (76.4% similarity with strain 59228). Full-length 16S rRNA sequencing resolved a globally conserved M. salivarium lineage from Saudi VAP patients, distinct from two divergent variants (S9 and S6). This approach provided insights into 16S rRNA sequence diversity and population structure, although whole-genome sequencing remains necessary for definitive strain-level discrimination and for clarifying the potential opportunistic role of M. salivarium in VAP. [IMPORTANCE] This is the first study to employ full-length 16S rRNA PacBio sequencing comprehensive phylogenomic characterization for 24 sequences of Metamycoplasma salivarium in ventilator-associated pneumonia populations. The results demonstrate 23 sequences (95.8%) exhibited 99.7%-99.9% similarity to reference strains NBRC 14478 (Japan), 59271 (USA), and PG20 (Sweden), indicating a genetically homogeneous population derived from a single evolutionary lineage circulating globally.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Association of treponemal chemiluminescent immunoassay signal intensity with TPPA reactivity in reverse sequence syphilis screening.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: [UNLABELLED] Reverse sequence screening for syphilis using treponemal chemiluminescent immunoassays (Tp-CIAs) is widely used in clinical laboratories; however, interpretation is typically based on binary cutoff values, and the clinical value of signal intensity remains underutilized. We conducted a retrospective diagnostic performance accuracy study including 1,827 individuals undergoing routine screening to evaluate the clinical utility of the Tp-CIA cutoff index (COI) as a continuous variable, using the TPPA as the reference standard. ROC analysis was performed to determine the optimal cutoff, and associations between COI values and TPPA reactivity were assessed. Tp-CIA demonstrated excellent discrimination of TPPA reactivity (area under the curve 0.992). COI values showed a strong monotonic association with TPPA reactivity (Spearman rs = 0.855), increasing from 2.5% at a COI <1 to 99.8% at a COI ≥30. An exploratory cutoff of COI = 3.25 increased specificity from 88.6% to 96.4%, with a corresponding decrease in sensitivity from 99.1% to 95.9%, compared with the manufacturer-recommended cutoff of 1.0. Discordant results (3.9%) were largely confined to low COI values, whereas high COI values were strongly associated with TPPA reactivity. Diagnostic performance remained consistent across HIV subgroups. Among individuals with concurrent non-treponemal testing, COI values were positively correlated with ordered rapid plasma reagin (rs = 0.637) and toluidine red unheated serum test (rs = 0.705) titer levels. These findings demonstrate that, within the analytical conditions of this study, higher assay-specific COI values were associated with a greater likelihood of TPPA reactivity. COI-based interpretation should remain supplementary to established confirmatory testing and clinical assessment; exploratory threshold requires independent analytical and clinical validation. [IMPORTANCE] Syphilis remains a growing global public health concern, and reverse sequence screening using Treponema pallidum chemiluminescent immunoassay (Tp-CIA) is widely adopted. Although these assays are interpreted qualitatively using manufacturer-defined cutoffs, the underlying signal intensity varies across specimens. In this study cohort, increasing Tp-CIA cutoff index (COI) values were associated with an increasing observed proportion of TPPA-reactive results. This association was assay- and cohort-specific and should be interpreted descriptively. COI should not replace established confirmatory testing, quantitative non-treponemal testing, or clinical assessment, and its potential supplementary value requires independent analytical and clinical validation.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Zebrafish float new hopes for fighting Vibrio cholerae with phage therapy.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: The increasing number of bacterial pathogens showing resistance against commonly used antibiotics has rendered currently available treatments alarmingly ineffective and has become a major public health issue. Phage therapy, using viruses that infect bacteria in a bacteria-specific fashion, is an alternative approach that has shown promising efficacy at killing multidrug-resistant species. However, understanding the basic mechanisms of bacteriophage biology poses substantial challenges. We are notably missing model systems to better comprehend phage-bacteria-human host interactions and to bridge the gap between in vitro research and clinical applications. In an article published in Microbiology Spectrum, Sidi Mabrouk et al. establish Danio rerio as a model to investigate bacteriophage-bacterium dynamics in a naturalistic context for Vibrio cholerae, an important human pathogen (A. Sidi Mabrouk, J. S. Depelteau, C. Foini, A. Kempff, et al., Microbiol Spectr 14:e03565-25, https://doi.org/10.1128/spectrum.03565-25). Leveraging key features of the zebrafish model, Sidi Mabrouk and colleagues highlight the complex interplay between the ICP1 bacteriophage, V. cholerae, and zebrafish-associated gut microbiome in the phage efficacy to clear the pathogen.

Microbiology Spectrum.title: Niche-specific transcriptional responses of Staphylococcus epidermidis during host colonization and infection.
Microbiology Spectrum.abstract: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a ubiquitous skin commensal but can act as an opportunistic pathogen causing foreign body-associated infections, including prosthetic joint infections (PJIs). The molecular mechanisms underlying this commensal-to-pathogen transition remain poorly understood. To investigate niche-specific transcriptional adaptations, RNA was isolated from nasal swabs and synovial fluid samples collected from patients with PJIs. Comparative quantitative real-time PCR was used to assess S. epidermidis gene expression in nasal samples, representing the colonizing niche, and synovial fluid, representing the infectious niche. Paired nasal and synovial fluid samples from individual patients were analyzed where available. The analysis focused on genes associated with virulence, adhesion, immune evasion, and metabolism. Three distinct expression profiles were identified: (i) a core profile, comprising genes with consistent expression in both niches, including immune evasion factors (capC, dltA, and mprF) and the adhesin sdrG; (ii) a niche-specific profile, comprising genes whose expression differed between niches, including increased expression of sdrH and the major autolysin atlE in synovial fluid; and (iii) a variable profile, comprising genes with heterogeneous expression patterns across patients, suggestive of strain- or patient-specific adaptation. Notably, central metabolic genes (fumC, gltA, and icd), together with agrC and its downstream target psmβ1, showed pronounced downregulation in synovial fluid. These findings provide direct ex vivo evidence for site-specific S. epidermidis gene expression during human colonization and PJI. They reveal distinct transcriptional patterns associated with adaptation to the colonizing and infectious environments and provide a basis for further investigation of potential targets for infection prevention and treatment.IMPORTANCEStaphylococcus epidermidis normally lives harmlessly on human skin but is also a major cause of infections involving prosthetic joints and other implanted medical devices. How this common bacterium adapts from colonization to persistent infection remains poorly understood. We compared S. epidermidis gene expression in nasal swabs, representing colonization, with that in synovial fluid from patients with prosthetic joint infections, representing the infectious niche. This patient-based comparison revealed distinct patterns of bacterial gene activity: some genes were consistently expressed in both niches, whereas others showed niche-specific changes.
